snippet.title: Portal 2 custom map "Magician's Boxes"
snippet.description:
I made a custom puzzle in Portal 2: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=143828949
IMPORTANT: YOU NEED TO ABUSE GAME GLITCHES TO COMPLETE THIS MAP.
This is an example walk-through of that map. Note that this is a SPOILER to the solution.
Cheats were NOT used.

Explanation (SPOILER): A reflector cube (lens cube) becomes a fixed point in space when a laser passes through it. If the cube is standing on a physics object, such as another cube, the supporting cube can be moved away and the lens cube will stay in air.
The lens cube will not be easily nudged, and if I recall correctly, it can even be stood on. It will only fall if the laser misses the cube, or if the level geometry under the box changes (portals, elevators etc).
THEORY: The game saves resources and excludes the lens cube from physics calculations once its velocity reaches zero. This way, the laser beams do not need to be recalculated frequently.

The development of Black Mesa began in 2004, after Valve had released a Source port of the original game, now called "Half-Life: Source". The port was really a lackluster compared to what it could have been, which spawned several community projects to do the port properly. That is how Black Mesa was born.
Black Mesa is not just a port or a clone of Half-Life. While it is a faithful reproduction of the original game, from scratch, with ramped up graphics and audio, many scenes were greatly expanded upon, improved, and even changed where the original made no sense. There are thousands of new models, hours of new voice talents, all very professionally constructed.

snippet.title: Portal 2 custom co-op map "Synchronized Flinging"
snippet.description:
I made a custom two-player puzzle in Portal 2: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=94468739
This is an example walk-through of that map. Note that this is a SPOILER to the solution.

This video was very difficult to record. This map is designed to be played by two players simultaneously, and there are very strict timers in the map that demand high degree of simultaneous coordination between the players.
I played this alone, controlling BOTH characters. The thing is: you cannot control both characters simultaneously. You have to switch between them constantly. To facilitate this at high accuracy, I used the "host_timescale" cheat, playing this at 10 % speed. This is why the movements are jerky at times. It is essentially a 10× sped up recording from how I played it.  I also utilized jumping extensively to preserve one character's velocity while controlling the other.

Finally, for some odd reason, the game decided to use a really high brightness level for this map.

snippet.title: NAO-robot unboxing / Finnish: Näin Nao tuli kotiin [w/subtitles]
snippet.description:
Postipaketista ilmestyi robotti. Videossa lisäksi Naon oma esittely. This is how I got my Nao. Video also contains Nao's Presentation. Subtitles included in English & Finnish!

The music from 7:45 onward is "A Twinkle", composed by Jcole for Assembly 1999. You can listen to it here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wjmpxidKR-o and download it here: http://www.scene.org/file.php?file=%2Fparties%2F1999%2Fassembly99%2Ftinymusic%2Fatwinkle.zip

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

----------
If you are interested in programming a humanoid robot, you can apply at http://developer.aldebaran-robotics.com/ . If you pass the tests (you need to prove your technical abilities and answer certain questions that profile you as a candidate), you will get the option to purchase your own Nao at a discount price, and join the Nao developer community, which seeks to develop real-life applications for a humanoid robot, for the eventual public release of the robot on market. The developer program is a contract which requires you to contribute to Aldebaran in certain ways.
Alternatively, there are several universities and research facilities around the world which have purchased Nao robots for research use. If you are in those academic circles, you may have the chance to program Nao robots there.

2014 addition: Apparently today Nao is available to the general public! You can buy your own Nao at: http://www.robotslab.com/Robot/NAO%20H25
The price is still much higher than it is with the developer program, but it is less than half of what it used to be.

Aldebaran is a French company, so most of the Nao developers are located in France, but there are plenty of them around the world, such as in USA, Japan, United Kingdom, Germany, and even a few here in Finland.
As of this video's release, Nao can speak over 20 different languages (well, more like it can enunciate those languages; its support for the actual text is still being improved), and understand many of them as well. My initial experiences with Nao's Finnish speech have so far surprised me.

P.S. I had charged and configured the robot before recording this video, to save time and avoid having to do it on camera. I also forgot to present on camera the DVD that was in the box.

snippet.description:
This is a followup to my previous video -- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RzEmjx7Pfsc .
In this video, I only hide those actors which would be occluding the dialog box that is to appear.
I implemented this feature in my Retranslation patch: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/cv2fin/ in version 2.1.0 and greater.

Played in FCEUX version 2.2.0.

The development of Black Mesa began in 2004, after Valve had released a Source port of the original game, now called "Half-Life: Source". The port was really a lackluster compared to what it could have been, which spawned several community projects to do the port properly. That is how Black Mesa was born.
Black Mesa is not just a port or a clone of Half-Life. While it is a faithful reproduction of the original game, from scratch, with ramped up graphics and audio, many scenes were greatly expanded upon, improved, and even changed where the original made no sense. There are thousands of new models, hours of new voice talents, all very professionally constructed.

snippet.title: Castlevania II: Let's kill Dracula with garlic
snippet.description:
What happens if you kill the undead Dracula in NES Castlevania II (Simon's Quest) with garlic? Let's find out! **WARNING** SPOILERS

This was recorded in my Finnish translation. https://iki.fi/bisqwit/cv2fin/
It includes my extended ending (with text from the original Japanese version; text which was NOT included in the North-American or PAL releases).

Note: This is not normally possible. The game robs you of all garlic the moment you enter the altar room. I used a RAM hack to keep them.

Recorded in nesemu1. See this video to learn about nesemu1: https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s
There is a small audio/video desync in this video, caused by using incorrect framerate in MEncoder call.

Apologies about the advertisement in the video, but YouTube identified the soundtrack of this video belonging to "one or more" copyright mafias, and to fund them it forces the advertisements.

snippet.title: Castlevania II / Simon's Quest Suomeksi / Finnish fan-translation ROM-hack
snippet.description:
Käänsin Simon's Quest -pelin suomeksi. URL: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/cv2fin/
This video showcases the Finnish translation that I created of Simon's Quest. The video contains sample parts from the translated game.

Besides just poking string data in, this translation project includes (among other things):
- Dynamic allocator / reorganizer for moving pointers and data around
- Map feature, coded in 6502 assembler, with dithered graphics automatically generated from an image edited in Gimp, with automatically chosen palettes and with sprites that improve the color resolution marginally
- Extended dialog box sizes
- String compression using existing (but unused) features within the original game
- Parameter-variant patch generation, such as whether to patch PAL or NTSC, whether to change the mapper into VRC6 or keep as MMC1, whether to extend this and that feature or not

Question: Do you want to see how it was made?

snippet.title: Black Mesa: Secret room under the stairs [Chapter: Questionable Ethics]
snippet.description:
This (0:33 onwards) is the hidden room. I used noclip. It is the only way to reach this room.
The beeps are a SSTV transmission. Part of Black Mesa ARG, in Portal style.
The horizontal/vertical partitioning (visual glitch) occurs because I spawned a large quantity of flashlights to illuminate the walls.
The "The Pizza is a LIE!" graffiti occurs dozens of times on a number of hidden walls throughout the game, for example inside some of those rooms you see during the tram ride in the beginning of the game. None of them are normally accessible; you have to use a map editor or the noclip cheat to see them.

The part in the beginning of the video is a scripted event. You hear it happening, but don't get to see. I used noclip to witness Dr. Horn's death first-hand. The actors in the room are just placeholders, though.

snippet.title: Black Mesa #10 Title Screen [~1 hour, HD] Background animation / attract mode.
snippet.description:
Something I enjoy in Valve's Half-Life series is the attention to detail. Though Black Mesa is a fan creation not made by Valve, it follows largely similar development principles.
The background graphics in the main menu is actually produced by the game engine itself, running as it does also during the game, animating a mock-up scene with many details.

I aimed to make a 10-hour video for this one (like I did with https://youtu.be/KbHQ-L4UJvA ), but settled for 1 hour because I needed to continue with making the LP.

You might set this video as a background image or something.

snippet.title: Black Mesa #0 Title Screen [11 hours!] Background animation / attract mode.
snippet.description:
Betcha you didn't expect that.
Something I enjoy in Valve's Half-Life series is the attention to detail. Though Black Mesa is a fan creation not made by Valve, it follows largely similar development principles.
The background graphics in the main menu is actually produced by the game engine itself, running as it does also during the game, animating a mock-up scene with many details.

I aimed to make a 10-hour video, but oops, it became almost 11 hours.

I uploaded this in 2048x1152 resolution in November 1st, 2012. Due to large staticity of the image, even when encoded in nearly lossless H.264 (crf=1, 30 fps), it ended up just 15 GB in size. Similarly the audio track was a lossless FLAC encode, measuring 3 gigabytes. The total was less than 20 GB, i.e. still within YouTube's upload size limits.
I intended to wait until YouTube has provided something better than 240p for it, but it had already been almost four weeks, so I went ahead and published it. I am eager to see when does the day come that YouTube provides something better than 240p for this video. Enjoy!
If you use the HTML5 player (go to "Try something new!" on the bottom of the page), you do get 480p though.

You might set this video as a background image or something.

snippet.title: Q&A - NESemu1 CPU explained (1000 subscriber special!)
snippet.description:
It is a special video time! This week my subscriber counter exceeded 1000, with Хозяин Снов being the 1000th. Thank you everyone!
One thousand! People like milestones, so I made a special video.
It also gave me a good opportunity to answer some semi-important and semi-urgent questions. More semi-important and more semi-urgent answers may be coming later, when you ask those questions. I cannot promise a schedule though.

In this episode, I cover my multilingual background and explain in detail how exactly the Ins() function in my NES emulator works. If you haven't seen the emulator yet, go and watch this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y71lli8MS8s .

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

In this video, I explain *how* did I come up with the short form for the Ins() function (which was actually automatically generated from data using the means described in this video).
However, I did not explain *why* I made it small. You can find _that_ explanation here: http://www.reddit.com/r/programming/comments/11au2d/a_while_back_a_fantastic_video_was_posted_of_an/c6l48cs

NEW: Additionally, if you absolutely must know, I expanded the very content of the #define macro of the Ins() function and covered the 8-bit encoding that I used in detail at https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/nesemu1/base256-explained.txt .

The background music is from One Must Fall! 2097, but with a twist! I downloaded a program that converts an MTM into a S3M, and then I created a program that converts a S3M into a multi-synthesizer MIDI suitable for playing with my ADLMIDI program, which plays MIDI using OPL3 emulation. This is thus played through FM synthesis. The original song uses PCM samples, but here you hear it in FM sound.

The headset that I am using here I acquired from DealExtreme for $6.80. You can find it here: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/dx/p/6217 It is rather good quality and a lot more convenient than the Sony hand-held microphone F-V120 that I have been using previously. It takes some practise to set the microphone in the exactly right position that it doesn't record my breath and that it captures at exactly the right volume, which is why there is some clipping in the narration of the programming part in the end.
The video camera is a Sony DCR-SR37 that is not actually mine. I used a single camera, a tripod mount, and no additional light sources.

The color correction, subtitling and editing was performed in kdenlive, using a SSH-tunnelled X11 session. I did the initial editing in EditStudio, because the SSH-tunnel does not carry sound. The audio was finally mixed in Audacity, and the final encode (and the logo in the beginning) was performed using my Hudmaker, my own program.


Currently, on most architectures, 64-bit is the largest available integer size. In this example I chose to use "72 instructions" as an example of a size that does not fit in an integer (and hence the hexadecimal numbers would not actually work without extra tricks, an example of which is shown in the very end). In the NES emulator, the number of opcodes was 259. I used 72 rather than 259 in this example, because I wanted the entire binary number to fit on the screen, for its cumbersomeness to be obvious.

You might wonder why I am saving in the editor so often. In many of my longer videos, I save dangerously infrequently. The reason is that I used the save function as an intentional visual delay about 2 seconds long each, to allow time for my narration. In my production toolchain (this is a tool-assisted education video), it is currently not possible to simply do nothing for a while, so I did the saving as an idle function. For my next videos I will try to devise some less distracting delay method.


The next part for Black Mesa Blind LongPlay will be coming tomorrow. After that, the schedule may be a little slower than previously because of the preparation for the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:33-44), but I still try to release an episode at least every third or second day.

snippet.title: Programming Arduino in C++11 -- ROM dumping
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video I show how to program an Arduino Atmega2560 board in C++11 to dump a ROM chip, such as a 386sx BIOS or a Famicom cartridge ROM. I also make a ZMODEM sender and a LED blinker in this video.

Sorry about the bad dub / lipsync in the beginning.  I recorded that part in a very noisy room, using a bad microphone (internal to the camera), and in another language, so I had to dub it over in postprocess -- which turned out to be considerably more difficult than I thought. Some year soon I might get a boom microphone for use in this kind of occasions.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

Please feel free to post comments & ask any questions / clarifications in the video comments. I try to reply to everyone when applicable. Please exercise clarity, politeness and good grammar, if you expect those values in the replies.

The EPROM chip pinout reference I used: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/epromread/eprom_pins.html
In particular, the 27C512 diagram here is applicable. For the NES ROM, I changed the OE/Vpp pin into address bit 16 and the CE/PGM pin into address bit 17.

I bought my Arduino board (which is a clone actually) from DealExtreme:
- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/dx/p/256335 (Feb 2014 update: The same board is no longer available in DX, but this is compatible with it and in the same price range.)
Presently it costs only about 15 EUR including shipping. 
The breadboard, the jumper wires and the resistors (for LED) are also from that shop. This pack includes all of those:
- bisqwit.iki.fi/dx/p/126383 (Feb 2014 update: Similar pack as the original one is no longer available.)
It also includes another Arduino board, but a smaller one (also clone) that does not have enough GPIO pins for ROM dumping, unless you use an external shifter microchip (such as 74LS595).
The three-color LED is:
- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/dx/p/135046

The operating system where I run the compiler and uploaded the program is Debian GNU/Linux, and I installed "arduino-mk" (which automatically installs the dependent avr-libc, gcc-avr, binutils-avr and arduino-core packages).
I edited the /usr/share/arduino/Arduino.mk file, changing the = into += on the lines that contain "CFLAGS=" and "CXXFLAGS=". Without this change, the C++11 option in my Makefile would be ignored.

The desktop environment shown in this video does not exist. It was created in postprocess to facilitate multi-file editing, which I have not previously used in my videos.

Related files and resources: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/epromread/

snippet.title: Booting Raspberry Pi the first time (well, almost)
snippet.description:
Today I received my copy of Raspberry Pi, a tiny and affordable PC. It measures smaller than 10x6x2 cm^3. But I have no USB keyboard, so I had to resolve to configuring the device through an SSH connection (which I did from the confines of my Linux-in-DOSBox hack, after configuring my server to grant DHCP addresses). I do have a USB mouse though, so I show the GUI for a short bit in the end.

I connected the device through its composite video* interface to an USB video adapter and recorded in PAL the process of booting up the device. The device was powered with a potato.

Well, not a potato, but a pebble. Pebble Portable Charger. Provides exactly the minimum required 750 mA at 5 V. I normally use it to power my MP3 player (Sansa Clip+) and a portable loudspeaker (SubSession Traveller 3) when I teach dances.

I edited the video with PiTiVi, a free video editing program which I am trying to learn, after spending some time with MovieChange's EditStudio, which provides slightly better set of features, but is not free.  The composite footage is unfortunately a bit over-exposed. But you can only record the "first time" only once, so that is too late to fix. There is also some strong color artifacting in the composite footage that I think was produced by a codec at a point or other.

*) The Raspberry Pi has HDMI output support, but I don't have HDMI input support in anything.

Sorry if this is meaningless content to some. I am actually making a programming video, and I promise to release it some day soon! :-)

If you want to order a Raspberry Pi, go to http://export.farnell.com/rp/order/ . The price depends on which country you order it to, but seems to vary between 35 USD and 39 GBP.

None of the product placements in this description were paid advertisements.

snippet.title: NTDec 5-in-1 cartridge: My only NES game ever.
snippet.description:
Though I am the founder of a website that used to be called NESVideos (today TASVideos), and I have invested countless hours of work into the development of NES emulators and the research of NES music, the truth is that I have only ever owned one (1) NES cartridge.*
Or rather, it is a Famicom cartridge. It is an unlicensed 5-in-a-1 cartridge by NTDec. It contains five small NES games. I still have that cartridge, and a console to go with it (which also is NTDec; a Famicom clone with PAL encoder).

In this video, I play through that cartridge on the real NTDec hardware (which is currently my only option, too: This cartridge has never been dumped onto PC), without any tool-assistance.

Here you can see that I am really just an average player. Personally I also note that years of TASVideos have not made me any better player than I were in the 20th century, when I last had a TV that would enable me to use the NTDec. (I just purchased a USB video input adapter a few days ago.)

I would have made this a let's-play, but I cannot think of anything interesting to say. And I would have had to speak in Finnish for it to be fluent in any manner, and then I would have had to subtitle it in English for the majority of my audience to understand. Too much work.

There is audio noise in this video. It is somehow generated by the game console, probably poor insulation somewhere. There is this saying that you get what you pay for, and that price may have been one of the strongest selling points for this device. Back then, a real NES was very, very expensive at least from the income viewpoint of my family.
(This NTDec is not my first one though. I broke the first one through bad soldering. I got this second one as a gift from a friend, and this is one of the first times I actually run it.)

*) I have played dozens of other NES games in the 1990s. In fact, I have played live almost all NES games released in Finland before some particular month & year. All were either played in friends' houses, in supermarkets or indoor amusement parks, or using NES consoles & games rented from video rental stores for a day or two.

snippet.title: EAN-13 barcodes demystified. Rendering in PHP.
snippet.description:
In this short tool-assisted education video, I illustrate how to render EAN-13 barcodes in software, and explain briefly how they are constructed.

I also render an UPC-A barcode.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

The EAN-13 barcodes are constructed of 12 digits + a check digit at the end. (I do not calculate the check digit in this example.) The _first_ digit (not the check digit at the end) determines the manner in which the next 6 digits are encoded.

In the american UPC-A, there are only 12 digits. It is actually a subset of the EAN-13, with the first digit of the thirteen assumed to be a zero. Since the function of the first digit in EAN-13 is to select the manner in which the barcode is encoded (and it does not actually produce any new lines), UPC-A codes and EAN-13 are visibly much alike, having exactly the same dimensions for instance.

Then there is EAN-8 which is 8 digits only, and UPC-E which has 6 digits only, but they work in the same or similar principles. You can find information about them in Wikipedia, and I do not cover them here.

The ISBN, used with books, is an EAN-13 code that begins with 978 or 979, and may have an additional 5-digit code after the main code.

Off-topic: It turns out that for a programmer, the hardest part in making these videos is in choosing the music. Yes, I had to create a barcode renderer; I had to create a Linux "emulator" (it's really just a console with vt100/Linux terminal emulation) for MS-DOS; I had to create software which renders this "window manager" that people have been asking questions about, entirely in postprocess; but the hardest part was in choosing music. This one is the Sunken Ship theme from Super Mario RPG, played through OPL3 emulation. On a MIDI player that I wrote, using a SPC to MIDI conversion process that I wrote. Reverb was added in postprocess in a software called Audacity, which I did not write.

Lossless downloadable 720x480 8-bit video (ZMBV + FLAC): https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/ean13/lossless_video.mkv

snippet.description:
In this video, I use a QuickBASIC program that I created and showcased last year in https://youtu.be/z2K-JBgM5lo . This time, I chose one very special and famous match from KGS Go Server's archives.

White player is Kim Myungwan, a Korean 8-dan professional (very, very strong).
The black player is called MoGo. He is a robot program running on a cluster of machines (800 CPUs total for about 15 teraflops).
In this game, Myungwan gives the robot 9 stones of advantage (handicap). The time setting is one hour for both players (sudden death, e.g. no byo-yomi).
In a shocking historic first, the robot wins by 1.5 poins. The game ended after 255 moves.
The match was played in August 2008.

An interesting side note is that Kim MyungWan used around 13 minutes while Mogo used about 55 minutes. Kim MyungWan is reported to have said that extra time would not have helped him.  (Source: https://senseis.xmp.net/?MoGo )

Note: Many players commenting on this game have obviously become stronger since this game was played (2008). Their comments are only shown here as citations, as part of the back-then original game observing performance, replayed by this program of mine.

There are some people who think that the audience should be completely silent (even going as far as hiding the kibitz window) while the game is in progress, and of course I am not fan of the "what's in your fridge" style chat that often goes on during the game, but I think in general, the kibitz is an integral part of the entertainment of watching the match, and often provides useful insight to the game, as long as the topic is about the game. The suspense and waiting for what's coming next (though one can only guess) is a significant factor in the entertainment. It is not nearly as entertaining to watch the game if you can simply click forward one move at time at your own pace. This is why I made this program play the game at its original pace.

snippet.title: Re: 256 colors is enough for everyone - 16 color version
snippet.description:
dakkiller1 requested to see a version of the 256-color starfield animation that only uses 16 select colors from the MCGA/VGA 262144 color palette.
Here it is. The only colors used in this video are (hand-picked, without much deliberation):

000000,FCFCFC,FC7800,7800FC
00FCA8,784400,440078,007844
342000,200034,003420,100800
080010,001008,A83400,3400A8
The low 3 bits of each color channel are zero, leaving only 6 bits per channel (64*64*64 colors).
Note that due to MPEG blurring, you may see other / smoother colors on the screen than that. Suggest you watch it at 720p level or higher.

Created with animmerger using the following commandline:

animmerger --noalign sfield-????.png -pc --gamma=2.2 -Dky --dc=16 --dr=3,8,16 -Q000000,FCFCFC,FC7800,7800FC,00FCA8,784400,440078,007844,342000,200034,003420,100800,080010,001008,A83400,3400A8 --gif=never -v -v

Where sfield-????.png are the frame-by-frame truecolor output files of the C++ version of the QBASIC program illustrated in the previous version. This invokation of animmerger produces 16-color PNG files, one for each frame, and with the following commandline I converted it into the .AVI file that I uploaded to YouTube:

mencoder -oac copy -sws 4 -vf scale=2560:1600 -mf fps=30 -ovc x264 -x264encopts crf=6:threads=4:me=umh:me_range=8:frameref=9 -o sfield_16color.avi -audiofile ../stream.dump mf://tile-%04d.png

snippet.title: Force-syncing a NES TAS: Simon's Quest in Finnish
snippet.description:
In this video I illustrate the result of force-syncing zggzdyp's Simon's Quest TAS (made with NTSC USA version) into a Finnish fan-translation made by me (95% complete).
It works quite nicely for the first 10 minutes, despite radically different dialog text timings, and then it desyncs. The place of desync is at a great swamp, but the cause of desync is undetermined.

The game uses extremely volatile randomness that depends on CPU & NMI timing.  Force-syncing involves recording the random seed & frame counter values using a conforming emulator, and then replicating those RAM contents each frame in the target emulator. Additionally, joypad input is recorded & fed at sites where the game polls the RAM variables storing the input data, rather than each frame within the NMI.

The TAS is: NES Castlevania II: Simon's Quest (USA) in 29:45.02 by zggzdydp.
Original publication: http://tasvideos.org/933M.html

snippet.title: Live tracing a NES emulator. Game: Mega Man 2
snippet.description:
In this extra installment to the emulator programming video of https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s , I show which areas of the emulator code are executed at each moment when the game is running. Best enjoyed on a 3200x1800 screen resolution or higher.

The entire source code of the emulator is shown on the left. (Though the text is only legible in the Original format.) Those areas which have been executed during the last rendered frame are lit in light blue. Each statement and expression is lit separately where possible, given compiler's limits to debugging information. Comments, declarations, and other syntactic parts that do not directly result in executable code are never lit.
Below the game window, is a map of the emulated system's RAM and ROM. Same rules apply. Yellow = written to.
On the bottom right, is a waveform display of the audio output of the emulator. And in the bottom right of the source code is a keypad display for the game console. An orange light indicates that the button was just pressed. The button presses come from a TAS.

Emulator: Nesemu1 © 2011 Joel Yliluoma -- Published at: https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s
Game: Rockman II © 1988 Capcom -- Published by Nintendo
Run: Tool-assisted speedrun © 2010 aglasscage, FinalFighter, pirohiko, & Shinryuu -- Published at: http://tasvideos.org/1649M.html
Compiler: icc version 12.1.2 © 2011 Intel
Debugger: ptrace system call © Linux kernel developers ;-)
Operating system: Debian GNU/Linux 64-bit © contributors

I used Intel's compiler, because it provides means (although contrived) to acquire expression-level tracing information over the executable file. With GCC, you can only acquire line-level tracing information. The actual process of obtaining an expression-level trace from the program's running was rather complicated, so I put all the resources related to it here, so others may possibly do similar presentations of their own small programs:
https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/nesemu1/trace/
I say small programs, because obviously the source code listings become huge and inconvenient with huge programs.

In hindsight: Wow, I expected a lot more variation. The most blinking seems to happen in sound code. A bit happens in the sprite conditions. Almost every other expression is pretty much executed every frame.

snippet.title: NES Memory Visualization: Mega Man 2
snippet.description:
You probably never wondered how NES games access the RAM & ROM they have available. Well, now you know!
The memory sections listed are, in order: internal RAM (2048 bytes) and ROM (262144 bytes).

In the visualization, all memory accesses decay in 1/3 seconds, so if there is some part that it lit, it has really been accessed during that frame. Surprisingly large areas of memory are used all the time. Blue = read; green = increased; red = decreased; yellow = both/neither increased and/nor decreased. White = Most recent write.

On the bottom, you can see an oscilloscope view of each of the signal generators used to produce sound effects and music.

On the right side, you can see the ROM tile bitmaps that the game uses. Those bitmaps that are currently within its mapped memory are rendered. Blue = tile was used as background graphics; white = tile was used as a sprite. Green = VRAM was read; red = VRAM was written to.

Apologies about the motion blurring I added. The original video framerate was about 60.1 frames per second, but YouTube clamps the framerate at 30 fps by _dropping_ frames until only 30 frames are displayed per second, which meant that if I want to display all the content, I would have to mix the frames together before uploading it. Believe it or not, the outcome is less noisy in appearance than it would have been without it.

The game is Rockman 2 (Mega Man 2's Japanese version).
The performance is tool-assisted speedrun by aglasscage, FinalFighter, pirohiko, & Shinryuu, in 23:48.51. More information: http://tasvideos.org/1649M.html

This video was recorded on an emulator that I created entirely from scratch. You can see the source code of that emulator here (showcased in 15 minutes): https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s

snippet.title: Hexomino game AI at different levels. (Like tetris, but with 6-block pieces.)
snippet.description:
In this video, I showcase how Pierre Dellacherie's Tetris AI fares with a mixed tetromino+pentomino+hexomino piece set. It is insanely difficult even for a human. Let's see how Pierre Dellacherie's AI fares without any customizations.

In addition to the 60 distinct hexominos, this particular game version also contains all 7 tetrominos and all 18 pentominos.
The playing field width was increased from 10 to 18 units, because otherwise the game is way too difficult. Furthermore, I ran the game on a 1.9 terahertz (1900 gigahertz) virtual machine in order to give the AI ample time to think. (I.e. I increased DOSBox's cycles count to the maximum it can go before it wraps to a negative value.)

In April 2011, I published the source code to a piece puzzle game here at YouTube. You can see it here: https://youtu.be/V65mtR08fH0
In addition to being playable, the game also had a built-in AI using a state-of-art real-time algorithm by Pierre Dellacherie, extended by me for multi-piece look-ahead. In this video and the others of this series, I explore the capabilities of that AI.

Final scores:

COM1: 4 lines on P2, 8 lines on P1
COM2: 10 lines on P2, 14 lines on P1
COM3: 4 lines on P2, 16 lines on P1
A significant part of the AI's failure happens when it accidentally rotates a piece that is on the ground and is unable to maneuver it back into the right position. Another problem is its inability to notice when a block simply cannot be moved horizontally through an obstacle. It usually leads straight to the gameover. Such aspects of gameplay were not addressed in Pierre's algorithm. Pierre's algorithm only provides evaluations for different placements; it is up to the implementor to determine which placements are possible to achieve and which are not. My implementation is slightly lacking in that regard, and this gameplay setting is very unforgiving for such mistakes.

I also explored some video techniques a bit. Sorry about that. I converted the VGA RGB video signal (simulated, of course) into an NTSC composite signal with 360 scanlines (letterboxed 480p widescreen), and then reconstructed it with an intentionally less-than-perfect scheme into an YIQ video signal, which was converted back into RGB (and then again to YUV for X264 encoding). I also simulated dot crawl by varying the colorburst phase on each scanline. The imperfect decoding scheme gave birth to a lot of horizontal chroma blurring, as well as to a faint perception of chroma dots. I was aiming for a VHS style effect. The commented source code of this conversion program is available at the address below. Reproduction of all these artifacts requires quite a high MPEG bitrate, which may mean that YouTube will have problem representing them unless you choose one of the HD quality levels.

snippet.title: Star Trek: Elite Force / RPG-X: How to remedy the broken neck syndrome
snippet.description:
The difference between using the mouse and the camera controls when observing your vicinity in RPG-X.

Sometimes -- once every few years I guess if I calculate the average -- I enjoy a good role-playing session. I'm not a fan of role-playing games such as D&D where you bring up the dice and the character sheets and stuff, or with BatMUD where everyone just mines for experience points and explores the game but does not really role-play, but I have always liked the concept of serious RPs where each player is an actor, and they together contribute towards a plot and make it as believable experience as possible for all the other players. For that, I recently discovered this RPG-X modification of Star Trek: Elite Force -- a game I have never heard of before and frankly not been really interested either -- and one of the thriving online communities built around it, The Last Outpost.
In an example RPG-X session, you might be playing a medic aboard the starship, developing medicines and scanning odd lifeforms while treating patients coming in for various injuries. Because none of that is really provided by the game mechanics -- for example, all of the supposedly injured player characters are usually in perfect health -- it is up to the players' imagination to create all the plot. It is a big game of pretend, and an entertaining one at that. The game engine does provide with authentic looking audio & visuals that enhance the experience. For example, when you're scanning the supposedly broken energy conduits in the walls with your tricorder, it looks exactly the same as if any character from actual Star Trek TV series was doing it. Aside from the fact that you're not really getting any readings whatsoever, nobody could tell that you're not really doing what you say you're doing. Then there is an extensive set of emotes that are simply choreographic macros your character might perform, to portray emotions, reactions and actions. Some macros include sounds, for example all the console-macros include console button pressing sounds, that are emitted regardless of whether you use the emote at a console or not.
It's kind of hard to summarize the whole experience and the attraction in few sentences though.

I guess this video is mostly targeted at TLO members, but I made it public so that others, whom it might interest, can possibly learn of the concept.

The purpose of this video is to teach the benefit of using the camera controls rather than moving the character's head around when you, as the player, want to see something without the intention of portraying the character as doing that.

The video was recorded with CamStudio.  Bad framerate, I know, cannot help it.

snippet.title: Half-Life: Source in low resolution [320x240]
snippet.description:
No, I did not make it 256 colors, but I did try out as an experiment how Half-Life would look like at 320x240, a very low resolution by today's standard but once rather standard for gaming.
There is no point to this video except to show how it looks like at 320x240.
One may immediately notice that the lack of antialiasing is rather distracting. Jagged edges of polygons, and what's more difficult to fix, moire artifacts in transparent textures such as the steel grid wall at 3:07. Adding proper antialiasing, for example by rendering in 4x size and then lanczos-rescaling to 320x200 with a slight sharpening factor, would improve the appearance dramatically.

snippet.title: Disk Defragmentation and Enfragmentation (FAT tool/toy)
snippet.description:
Do you frequently defragment your disk, only to find that the file system does not need defragmentation, thereby ruining your tech-oriented mood? I present you, the Enfragmentation tool. It fragments the filesystem, so that defrag can be run again.
It is a meaningless toy that I wrote in 1998. I never released it, and consequently never bothered to fix some bugs in it. In this video I ran it three times for extra gusto, and on the third time it damaged some innocent file that Microsoft Scandisk fixes to the best of its abilities. Enfrag also never updates the second FAT table, so Scandisk/chkdsk/dosfsck always has to fix it after Enfrag has been run.

Microsoft Windows 3.11 (Windows for Workgroups) also makes an appearance. I run it in the beginning to show how system-oriented stuff used to be managed from MS-DOS rather than from Windows, and in the end to show that things still work. QBasic Nibbles crashes because the computer is too fast.

Implementation language: Borland Pascal
Source code: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/enfrag.pas and executable (enfrag.exe)
Provided AS-IS. If you destroy your files with it, I won't be held responsible. Also, it only works for FAT12 and FAT16 volumes (not FAT32, not NTFS).

P.S. There is no sound in this video. Normally, when you defragment the disk, you will hear a lot of noise from your harddisk that provides the aural entertainment to counterpart the visual entertainment, but because this video was created in a virtual machine, there was no harddisk that would make the noises. I could have simulated them in post-process, but there is a limit to the amount of expenditure of effort even for me...

snippet.title: Creating a NES emulator in C++11 (PART 1/2)
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video I create a NES emulator with C++0x. ENABLE CAPTIONS!
The emulator is very accurate, and sort-of portable; it compiles on any architecture that support libSDL, but it outputs audio through an external program and reads joypad input from a file.
This video is part 1/2.
-- Part 1 ( https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s ): Creating the emulator.
-- Part 2 ( https://youtu.be/XZWw745wPXY ): Compiling and running.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

The source code is about 940 lines in total.
Download & FAQ & resources: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/nesemu1/

Approximate count of lines of code per topic, in the source code:

- 20 lines, CPU: Declarations (registers, flags and internal memory)
- 100 lines, CPU: Interpreting and executing CPU opcodes & signals
- 100 lines, CPU&GamePak: Memory mapping (iNES mappers 0,1,2,3,7 are supported)
- 40 lines, PPU: Declarations (registers and emulator-specific status variables)
- 50 lines, PPU: Memory mapping and I/O
- 180 lines, PPU: Rendering and timing control
- 30 lines, PPU & IO: Joypad updating (PPU provides the timing for input-file access)
- 40 lines, PPU & IO: Color NTSC emulation (converting NES colors into RGB through NTSC modem)
- 15 lines, IO: libSDL initialization and rendering
- 35 lines, main&IO: ROM loading from file, initialization and emulation loop
- 200 lines, APU: Sound emulation (of which 40 lines are because of DMC/DPCM support)
- 130 lines, (other, such as comments, and inaccuracies in the above numbers)

Check out MaiZure’s excellent walkthrough of the source code of the emulator from this video!
http://www.maizure.org/projects/decoded-bisqwit-nes-emulator/

Background music: Jinguuji detective series. It was difficult to choose. I wanted good NES music, but I did not want it to too recognizable. I intended to convert something, but I had already spent months on this video... It was getting late.

Because of the 15 minute limit that YouTube was imposing on my account when I made this video, I had to develop many techniques to shorten the code dramatically. I also had to type it very quickly… And I had to split the actual demonstration into a second video.

I use C++11 exclusive techniques extensively in the code. I am particularly proud of the CPU emulator. It is cycle and memory access accurate, and feature-complete. It is not very slow, either. It is only 100 lines long, thanks to a number of clever ideas. I thank byuu for a particular idea that helped make it horizontally shorter. Each if() in ins() is completely parsed and evaluated at compile-time. Effectively the compiler synthesizes 259 distinct ins() functions, each performing only the particular opcode's worth of work.

I architected all the components in as close conformance as I could to whatever documentation I found on nesdev.com regarding how they work. There may be a few minor shortcuts that I took in order to avoid the trap of investing 90 % of source code to fix a problem that affects 10 % of games.

In design, my primary guideline was that the _hardware_ was always designed for simplicity (with regards to chipspace consumption). Most compact design that gets the work done. This means that any extra-ordinary complex behavior and myriad details by the hardware arises from simple design. I always tried to replicate that simplicity in my emulator. I think I managed quite well in that regard. It is not perfect though: It does not pass _all_ tests by Blargg, and some games that should run, outright crash at start. But the compatibility according to my tests is still very high, and interestingly, many TASes made with FCEUX run also on my emulator.

Note that creating an emulator is perfectly legal. I wrote all the code from scratch; it comes from my mind, and is therefore entirely my copyright; it is not anyone else's copyright. I believe that programming is art, and my code is my means of expressing myself. There exists no legislation that prohibits anyone from e.g. printing this source code on a t-shirt (assuming that *I* gave permission to that).  I am also not selling this as a product, i.e. even in the dystopian event that I should happen to be using algorithmic methods that someone else has previously patented against every notion of conscience and wisdom, I am still not infringing on any patents. Or so I believe.

snippet.title: Trails of Cave Story: Synthesizing music
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted programming video I create a synthesizer from scratch. It plays authentic Cave Story (洞窟物語) music tracks and sound effects (ORG and PXT files).

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

All resources concerning this video can be downloaded from https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/doukutsu-org/ , including the patch that does the waveform visualization.
Note there's a small bug in the showcased program regarding pitch calculation. It appears to work only when the sample rate is 48000. The formula for calculating "scale" for the lanczos filtering was also wrong; it used "phaseacc" when it should have used "phaseinc". The version on the web page has both bugs fixed.

The music system -- called Organya -- works like this. The song has 16 channels, eight of which are for melodic instruments and the other eight are for drums only.
Each channel is assigned one instrument, which is defined in the song header, and cannot be changed during the song.
Each channel can have a maximum of 1 voice playing simultaneously.
There is a global "wave table", which is hardcoded into the game; the wave table contains 100 short wave samples; the instruments refer to this wave table.
The actual song data is a per-channel list of events. Each event can begin a note, which plays for duration, or it can change the amplitude of the sample playing on the channel, or it can change the pan level, or do all of above.

In this program I play the music through ALSA sound system in Linux. For no reason at all, the audio data is going to be floating-point as opposed to the more commonly used sixteen-bit or eight-bit integer audio.

All the background music, in this video, is actually played through the program that I am writing in this very video. The background music played during programming is composed by Motoi Sakuraba, and originally published in Tales of Phantasia and Star Ocean SNES games. I converted those music tracks into Organya songs (covers).

The in-game songs I play are:
-- 3:56 Bush Lands (note: Grasstown is a mistranslation; note: played here without percussion)
-- 8:21 Jenka (note: it's a Finnish folk dance type, letkajenkka)
-- 8:59 Outside (the song that plays in the scene where you might choose to get the "bad ending")
-- 10:59 Gestation (the "default" exploration theme that plays in the beginning)
-- 12:36 Geothermal (this plays on the entrance of the first major boss, where the plot too begins branching significantly: it decides what happens to miss Curly Brace.)
-- 14:26 Pulse (demonstrating the detuned instruments; waveform is of "safety" though)
-- 14:55 Fanfare 1 (acquiring an item)

I do some tool-assisted voiceover in the video. I had fun doing that, not taking my cumbersome pronunciation too seriously. I hope you won't, either. All is fair in teaching memorably. Well, I _cannot_ take it too seriously. English is very difficult to pronounce for me, very difficult sequences of consonants and sometimes hard to choose the right phonemes to begin with. In Finnish, my native language, having more than two consonants in a row is very rare, and even when there are two, the possible combinations are very few. I have been training my English pronounciation for years, but the entire language is a tongue-twister for someone with this background. I have found Hebrew and Japanese to be significantly easier.
Anyway, does anyone want to contribute closed-captions?

Quick illustrations of each modulation method (each generates 8-bit mono PCM audio):
No modulation example code:
(add relevant #includes)
int main() { float p=0;for(;;) { float a = sin(p); putc(128 + 100*a); p += 0.1; } }
Amplitude modulation is like this: The level of one signal is multiplied by the level of the second signal. Example code below:
int main() { float p=0,p2=0;for(;;) { float a = sin(p), b = sin(p2); putc(128 + 100*a*b); p += 0.1; p2 += 0.01;} }
Frequency modulation is like this: The frequency of one signal is changed by the level of the second signal. Example code below:
int main() { float p=0,p2=0;for(;;) { float a = sin(p), b = sin(p2); putc(128 + 100*a); p += 0.1 * (1+b/9); p2 += 0.1;} }

snippet.title: NES Memory Visualization: Mega Man [Revision 2]
snippet.description:
You probably never wondered how NES games access the RAM & ROM they have available. Well, now you know!
The memory sections listed are, in order: internal RAM (2048 bytes); ROM (131072 bytes).

In the visualization, all memory accesses decay in 1/3 seconds, so if there is some part that it lit, it has really been accessed during that frame. Surprisingly large areas of memory are used all the time. Blue = read; green = increased; red = decreased; yellow = both/neither increased and/nor decreased. White = Most recent write.
On the right side, you can see an oscilloscope view of each of the signal generators used to produce sound effects and music.

Be sure to watch in HD. This video was uploaded in 3416x1920 resolution, and for this once, it was not just because of pixel scaling! The game was really rendered in 1920p...
You might wonder: How does that make sense? Well, remember that in analog television, theoretically, the horizontal resolution is infinite. Here, I went the extra mile and actually simulated the NTSC signal processing at very high resolution to produce a quite authentic looking picture. It is not a mere video post-processing gimmick: The emulator really produces composite NTSC signal _only_ (i.e. no paletted RGB pixels), which is then decoded in order to produce image. This is relevant, because though the pixel resolution of the NES is just 256 horizontally, the NTSC signal generator actually produces signal that shifts a little on each scanline, and mixes adjacent pixels together by outputting pixels on a sub-wavelength precision. The actual horizontal resolution of the signal ends up being 2048, plus what may be required to reproduce signal degradation artifacts.
Apologies about the motion blurring I added. The original video framerate was about 60.1 frames per second, but YouTube clamps the framerate at 30 fps by _dropping_ frames until only 30 frames are displayed per second, which meant that if I want to display all the content, I would have to mix the frames together before uploading it. Believe it or not, the outcome is less noisy in appearance than it would have been without it.

The game is FC ロックマン (NES Mega Man).
The performance is tool-assisted speedrun by Joel Yliluoma, a.k.a. Bisqwit, in 15:38.07. More information: http://tasvideos.org/726M.html
IMPORTANT: In order to fit in YouTube's 15 minute limit, I condensed the video a little. Small sections of the video were SPED UP. The playing is authentic, but the presentation is sped up. The true completion time from power-on to end of input was 15:38.07.

This video was recorded on an emulator that I created entirely from scratch. You can see the source code of that emulator here (showcased in 15 minutes): https://youtu.be/y71lli8MS8s

snippet.description:
Portal 2 challenge mode map "column blocker" solved with 4 portals and 256 colors in 424x240 resolution.

My computer is slow, and the challenge mode does not allow recording with host_timescale, so the scripted elements (including the movement of the cube when moved around) are jerky. It is a glitch in the demo player of the Source engine. It occurs when a demo is replayed at a higher framerate than it was recorded on.


What?
I create videos like this. If you did not like it, please unsee it and watch something else instead.
Though in all seriousness, this is not really what I planned on publishing next. I just did it for fun. I'm working on something that takes a bit of time.

Gameplaywise, it is not a particularly special video either. In fact, many have solved this room in 2 portals. However, I have never mastered the "bunny hop" technique required for jumping over large gaps, so I only did the "clever" part of optimizing the portal count and forfeited the "nimble" part that is not my specialty.

The demo was recorded at 640x480 resolution with lowest possible settings so that it could be recorded with maximal rate (given the lack of host_timescale). Then I replayed it in 848x480 using highest possible settings, at a constant 30 fps rate (host_framerate and startmovie). I did not use a higher resolution, because I was going to downscale it to 424x240 anyway. I did not use a higher frame rate, because it would have aggravated further the demo replaying bugs of the Source engine. Then I downsampled it into 424x240 using lanczos filter for spatial scaling implemented in MEncoder; and dithered it using Yliluoma-2 positional dithering algorithm implemented in Animmerger, with a dynamic 256-color palette chosen with Neuquant neural network quantization algorithm implemented in Animmerger. The palette is constant for every 500 frames.  (So it changes a total of 10 times during the video.)

snippet.title: Creating music in one line of C code
snippet.description:
In 1999 I experimented a bit with creating a minimal C program that can create music. Here is the source code and the music. Admittedly it is more than 1 line (four 80-character lines to be precise in its original layout, including comments; seven 40-character lines in this updated format, excluding comments), but both can be formatted into one line each less than 256 characters (with comments removed).

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

I posted this because there is currently an ongoing challenge on creating entertaining music with C oneliners. You can see examples here:
- http://countercomplex.blogspot.com/2011/06/16-byte-frontier-extreme-results-from.html (background)
- https://youtube.com/watch?v=GtQdIYUtAHg&feature=related (viznut's round 1)
- https://youtube.com/watch?v=qlrs2Vorw2Y&feature=related (viznut's round 2)
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCRPUv8V22o (viznut’s round 3)
- http://wurstcaptures.untergrund.net/music/ (online test facility, limited syntax)
- http://tasvideos.org/forum/p/289092#289092 (TASvideos thread and more links)

P.S. Creating programming videos that can not only be enjoyed perfectly in 240p, but also in 120p, is not an easy task. 90p is still legible if you use a lanczos rescaler (bicubic blurs it too much).

Explanation of the second code:

The song is 64 frames long. The for-loop C counts frames from 0..63, wrapping back to 0 after 63. On each frame, a note may be triggered or not triggered.
o will be assigned the frequency value for channel 1 by taking the song character corresponding to C/8, and calculating 99*pow(89/84, n) where n = 99 minus the character. 89/84 happens to be a very good approximation of 2^(1/12), the ratio between the frequencies of two successive half-steps in equal temperament tuning. The actual exponentiation is performed by multiplying o with 89/84 for each loop iteration where the decreasing k still is larger than the value of the character.
f will be assigned similarly from channel 2 (the index is now C rather than C/8).
Then, 8-bit PCM samples will be produced for 999+99*(C&2) times. The alternating *99*2 is there to bring some swing to the rhythm: each frame is alternatingly either 999 or 1197 samples long, with the alternation switching every two frames. The samples are generated using a formula s*(a(f) + b(o)), where s is the PCM sample counter (which acts as amplitude), a(f) is a formula that generates a simple waveform for channel 2, and b(o) is a formula that generates a simple waveform for channel 1. The constant 776 in the formula is used to compare the frequency to the frequency corresponding to the character '%', which stands for silence.

Each PCM sample is a 8-bit integer, which represents the air pressure that varies 8000 times in a second. Periodical variations in the pressure are perceived by ears as sound; the more frequently (faster) it varies, the higher the perceived pitch is. The actual value of the pressure is irrelevant; the ear only perceives the changes, not the values themselves. However, the larger the variations are, the louder the perceived volume is.The speaker attached to the computer is a device which attempts to reproduce the air pressures by moving an electromagnet-driven membrane back and forth, in order to produce the sounds.

This program produces the PCM samples with the mathematical formula, and then outputs them by simply issuing the putchar() function. If the program was run as-is, it would appear to spew garbage to the display. The proper way is to redirect its output into the speaker. In Linux/Solaris systems with Open Sound System, redirecting the audio to /dev/dsp accomplishes that task. On other systems, you may need to pass the audio data to another program, such as aplay or MPlayer, either directly through a pipe, or through an intermediate temporary file. On Cygwin/Mingw for instance, you can do this: ./sig2a.exe | mplayer -demuxer rawaudio -rawaudio rate=8000:channels=1:samplesize=1 -

8-bit 8000 Hz audio is rather low quality; today the most commonly used type of audio definition is 16-bit 44100 Hz, which means that it has 2^16 (65536) distinct pressure levels that can be varied at most 44100 times in a second. An 8-bit integer can represent only 2×2×2×2×2×2×2×2, that is 2^8 = 256 distinct pressure levels.

snippet.title: Portal2 with HDRI [combating the greyness!]
snippet.description:
Portal 2 is a grey game. I was going to create another dithering demonstration video and use Portal 2 as the source material, but Portal 2 is so grey that it was rather unfit to be rendered on the platform that only has RGB extremes. So I thought, I would combat this problem by applying a HDRI transformation on each image frame of the video. It would bring out the contrast and the color.
Every image frame of this video has been treated by a pfstmo_fattal02 tone mapping operator (mix 70 % of it and 30 % of the original).

I used mr. Fattal's tone mapping operator in this video because I like its apperance. It has some shortcomings and there are probably better ones, but I liked it, so I used it. And I know it increases the colorfulness a bit. But still the result was too grey, so I could not use it. Instead of discarding it entirely, I decided to publish it as-is.


I wrote more stuff here originally, but Firefox crashed during the upload (out of memory), and my text was lost entirely, and the upload was cancelled as well (despite the hyped "resumable uploads" of YouTube's "advanced uploader"). I had to retype what I remembered having written earlier. Too bad.

I hate this Wheatley overlay by the way. He is not even a carried object. Switch to the third person mode, and you see he is not even there. He cannot collide with walls, and he cannot be dropped. He's just a camera obstacle. Which is really annoying when you are trying to play a camera man.

P.S. I keep running into Raanan Fattal in various contexts. The many papers he has co-authored are mostly interesting reading, at http://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~raananf/ .

snippet.title: Half-Life 2 on the EGA (PC)
snippet.description:
This video shows how Half-Life 2 WOULD appear, if rendered through the EGA, 640x350 resolution. The audio is original from the game (upscaled by 5% to match the video speed), however rendered through 1.19 MHz 6-bit pulse width modulation, as though from the PC speaker, though somehow stereo.
(Note: YouTube blurs both the video and the audio severely. I can't help it. Try watching it in the highest definition your computer can replay.)

Video technical specs: 640x350 pixel resolution; fixed 16 color palette (hardware-assigned, standard default selection from the 64 choices); each pixel can be assigned separately from the palette of 16 colors. I did not change the default palette.

Note: The EGA palette is heavily biased towards bright colors, meaning that when trying to represent anything dark, you have two options: either completely black, or some combination of gray pixels. Which is why this video appears rather black at places.

snippet.title: Half-Life 2 on TMS9929A (TI-99/4A, ColecoVision, MSX etc.)
snippet.description:
This video shows how Half-Life 2 WOULD appear, if rendered through the TMS9929A chip, which was used in TI-99/4A, ColecoVision, and in the MSX (I/O & CPU speed disregarded). In addition, the audio was rendered through the SN76494 soundchip, which was used in TI-99/4A, Tandy 1000, and in the MSX.
(Note: YouTube blurs the video severely. I can't help it.)

Video technical specs: 256x192 pixel resolution; fixed 15 color palette (hardware-assigned, non-reassignable); for every 8x1 section only 2 distinct colors can be used.
Audio technical specs: Three square wave channels, each with separately adjustable volume in (0..15) range and pitch in 110..115000 Hz range; one noise channel with three distinct noise patterns and adjustable volume. This synthesizer varies the pitch&volume parameters of each channel 40 times per second, using an FFT-matching iterative heuristic algorithm, to produce the closest possible representation of PCM signal. Very surprisingly, the speech rendered by this system is actually understandable.

Here's the source code of the program I used to treat the audio: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/audio_transform_tandy.cc Instructions on use are included in the file.

snippet.title: Creating a MicroBlaze emulator in C++11 (runs Linux!)
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted programming video, I create a portable emulator for a certain architecture that can run Linux, using C++11. The source code is about 780 lines in total.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

Approximate count of lines of code per topic, in the source code:

- 80 lines, CPU: Registers and constants
- 230 lines, CPU: Interpreting and parsing CPU opcodes
- 80 lines, CPU: Exceptions and Interrupts
- 100 lines, CPU: Memory Management Unit (MMU)
- 50 lines, I/O framework: Memory map, endianness and integer sizes
- 50 lines, Device: UART (console I/O)
- 60 lines, Device: Timer
- 50 lines, Device: Interrupt Controller
- 20 lines, Loading of Linux kernel from disk file
- 60 lines, (other, and inaccuracies in the above numbers)

All resources concerning this video can be downloaded from https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/microblaze/ .

I do not own a MicroBlaze chip, nor any FPGA platform by Xilinx or anyone else.
I just wanted to create an emulator that can run Linux, inspired by Fabrice Bellard's JSLinux at http://bellard.org/jslinux/ .

For the emulator programming example that I wanted to create, I started looking for the simplest possible platform that can run Linux, and from reading GXemul source code, I initially went with DEC Alpha.
However, after writing most of the CPU emulator for Alpha, I perceived that by adding the remaining parts, such as PALCODE emulation, the emulator easily grows far beyond what people could read and understand in 15 minutes (YouTube's currently enforced limit on my account). Thus I gave up with DEC Alpha.

Then, when studying QEMU source code, I learned about MicroBlaze.
I downloaded the official documentation of MicroBlaze, and found that it was possible to emulate it with a relatively few lines of code.
I had the kernel up and booting in a few days, but I ran into serious problems when trying to get userspace programs work. Turns out, the GNU toolchain for MicroBlaze is not as robust as I thought it would be. I won't enumerate the exact list of problems I had, but metaphorically speaking, I spent two weeks wading a poisonous swamp, trying to find a way around thorny bushes that seemed to extend for miles in all directions. It was quite exhausting.
Thanks to the MicroBlaze target GCC maintainer, Michael Eager, for being patient with me and my many questions and/or complaints.
In the end, I settled for less-than-perfect and this is what you have. After all, my focus was in the emulator, not in Linux...

Examples on how the MicroBlaze CPU differs from Intel 386/Pentium family (x86):
- Many categories of instructions are optional, even ones that have been always present on x86.
- All instructions are 32 bits in length (with an optional 32-bit prefix for long immediates). In x86, instructions are of varying lengths.
- All memory access must be properly aligned. In x86, only a handful of SIMD instructions require memory addresses to be aligned.
- MicroBlaze is big-endian (12345678h is stored in memory as 12 34 56 78). x86 is little-endian (78 56 34 12). There is also a little-endian version of MicroBlaze.
- MicroBlaze has instructions with a "delay slot", where a branch/return will not take immediately effect, but after one extra instruction. x86 does not have delay slots.
- Support for "flags" is very minimal. Only a handful operations support the carry flag. With x86, almost every operation affects the zero, sign, carry and other flags.
- Floating point functionality is greatly reduced, and in fact, optional. In x86, the FPU is built-in (since Pentium), and supports more precision.
- The TLB is software-managed, by the kernel software. In x86, it is hardware-managed from the paging tables that are stored in system RAM.

Apologies if the text's tininess bothers anyone. From my previous videos I received feedback suggesting that I should try to maintain a broader visual to the source code rather than zooming in at times for focus, so I did exactly that. I also experimented with some ways to keep the aspect ratio natural even as it varies. Tip: HD.
The ending cuts a few seconds short due to an unidentified encoding mishap. I put the text in annotations instead.

The music in this video is played through ADLMIDI using OPL3 emulation.
The songs are from SNES games Thunder Spirits, Bahamut Lagoon and Fire Emblem 4.

I do some tool-assisted voiceover in the video. I had great fun doing that, not taking my cumbersome pronounciation too seriously. English is very difficult to pronounce, very difficult sequences of consonants and sometimes hard to choose the right phonemes to begin with. I have found Hebrew and Japanese to be significantly easier.
Anyway, does anyone want to contribute closed-captions?

snippet.title: Portal 2: Game begin in 3rd-person mode (free camera)
snippet.description:
This video shows the beginning of the first chapter of Portal 2, viewed in third-person perspective (Chell is shown on camera).

Apologies about the lack of programming videos lately! I'll get back to it soon, but for a while I've been fascinated with this stuff.

NOTE ABOUT CHEATS: Because Valve cheated somewhat with the implementation of the container ride scene, I also had to cheat in order to capture the performance.
Explanation: The entire timespan in the game beginning from the moment Chell wakes up the second time and ending to the moment the container "docks" in the wall, Chell is _physically_ located in a cold steel room that is completely separated from the rest of the facility. The game cheats by translating her "eyes" to the inside of the container that Wheatley is maneuvering. The cold steel room contains the same physical geometry as the wrecked room, although greatly simplified. It is used for handling the collisions of Chell's character to the rest of the world, which are greatly simpler to handle than the continuously changing space within the container (where even the floor tilts).
When Chell is viewed in the third person, the camera actually fixates on the location where Chell _really_ is, rather than what she's seeing with the first-person camera. This is why the third-person camera shows the cold steel room. This surprised me greatly.
Because I really wanted to show the container ride from an outside perspective, I had to cheat and grant Chell the power of flying and no-clipping with the "noclip" console command.
The container that Wheatley drives is actually non-tangible, so it is not even possible to put Chell inside it and let her land. She will fall through the floor immediately. Thus, I could not find a way to capture a 3rd-person view of Chell within the container without using the noclip mode.
When the container finally "docks" in the wall, the game teleports Chell's physical body into the container by mathematically adding a numeric offset to her coordinate within the map. However, because in this video she was no longer within the cold steel room when that teleportation happened, she ended up being teleported to a completely different location: Near the background painting cube of the scene. I had to fly her back to where the plot happens.

I first attempted to create this video by overriding the camera paths with the "camera smoother" facility of the "demoui" dialog box in Source. However, doing so also took Chell with the camera, so I had to forget about using the camera smoother. For some reason, the game assigns Chell's location relative to the camera rather than the other way around. If I tried to put the camera in an upper corner of the room, suddenly Chell was also there, head poking through the ceiling.
Instead, I controlled the camera angles by toggling the "thirdperson_mayamode" setting on and off (with the "edit" option of demoui) and occasionally adjusting the "cam_idealdist" setting.

The container ride has a number of weird properties that probably arise from it being pre-calculated. For instance, I first tried to capture this demo entirely at 90 frames/second rate. This ended up with the physics within the scene being incredible jagged and sometimes even failing to happen. (You can see it here:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kNSHhcKzfjc ). Because I did not want to lose the smooth quality of the rest of the video, I recaptured that part at 30 frames/second rate and spliced it into this movie. This solution worked nicely with only minor glitches remaining (such as Wheatley's entire dialog subtitles being flashed in a few seconds before the container ride begins, and the container seemingly teleporting at 3:39. Judging from my camera angles, the crate did not teleport when I recorded the movie).

Rendered in 1366x768 at max settings (hardware antialias not supported), lanczos-scaled up to 1920x1080 for YouTube to enable the 1080p option.

Other notes: The pristine "hotel hell" and the time-torn "hotel hell" are both located within the same map, of course, along with the cold steel room. However, to save rendering resources, the game actually vanquishes almost all furniture from the original room when it teleports Chell into the other room. You can see the stripped room in this video at 3:00. I land there because I need to jump _somewhere_ in order for advance the plot, and I cannot do that in the ruined room because it is nontangible.
