snippet.title: Half-Life 2 in low resolution [320x240]
snippet.description:
No, I did not make it 256 colors, but I did try out as an experiment how Half-Life 2 would look like at 320x240, a very low resolution by today's standard but once rather standard for gaming.
There is no point to this video except to show how it looks like at 320x240.
One may immediately notice that the lack of antialiasing is rather distracting. Jagged edges of polygons, and what's more difficult to fix, moire artifacts in transparent textures such as the steel grid walls. Adding proper antialiasing, for example by rendering in 4x size and then lanczos-rescaling to 320x240 with a slight sharpening factor, would improve the appearance dramatically. (I tested.)

There is a visual glitch in mr. Breen's video screen, somehow caused by this low resolution. It did not appear at 1024x768 when I tested. My guess is that Valve forgot to add a call to the function, glViewPort (or SetViewport in case of DirectX), when rendering into the texture for the display, causing the texture to be inadvertedly clipped to the display boundaries.

snippet.title: Half-Life 2 attract mode / main menu
snippet.description:
Something I enjoy in Valve's Half-Life series is the attention to detail. The background graphics in the main menu is actually produced by the game engine itself, running as it does also during the game, animating a mock-up scene with many details.
There are many interesting bits of dialog recorded for the game that are only replayed during this attract scene, such as the line that reminds combine soldiers that every 100 "neutralized" citizens gives them the privilege to sex (albeit still not for reproduction). I don't understand why they went with prerendered animations instead in Portal 2.

snippet.title: Portal 2: 1up controls both co-op bots in: mp_coop_paint_red_racer [PC split-screen]
snippet.description:
This video shows another way to solve this stage of Portal 2 Co-operative challenge. I have noticed that everyone has different solutions for passing the cube to the jumping player. On that tangent, I wanted to devise more (maybe contrived) solutions.

Note: I sometimes forgot that I was playing in timescale mode, so you may need to watch the video in slow motion to be able to follow all that happened. Sorry about that. (However, even at 0.1 timescale mode it is difficult to control both characters at once. The game only accepts input to one of them at time, thus creating a pressure to rush things.)

For a satisfying quality, I recorded this video at 2048x1024 (aspect ratio 2:1), 240 fps into ~27000 individual uncompressed TGA files. Because I quickly ran out of disk space that way (laptop harddisks are small, and with Source it is not possible to save to other location than the predefined one), I also ran in Cygwin a script which continually transferred the TGA files across network to another computer (making tar.lzop files of them and using scp -c blowfish-cbc).
On the Linux server the files were transferred into, the TGA files were combined into a single 30 fps recording using a series of scripts. The first script simply combines the files from each package into 240 fps HuffYUV AVI files. The second script combines those AVI files into a raw RGB stream; the third one upscales it into 4096x2048 using a lanczos filter (in order to enable the 1080p quality level in YouTube), and the fourth script reduces the framerate into 30 by weighted averaging the frames with a gaussian curve. Then the fifth one encodes the video using x264, and the sixth one adds ogg-encoded soundtrack, producing the 740 megabyte MKV file that was uploaded to YouTube. Many of these steps were done in parallel by utilizing a concept called "pipes", without intermediate temporary files.
240 fps is admittedly a bit of overkill. Maybe 180 fps would be enough.

Because my desktop is actually only 1366x768 in size, I had to create and extend the Windows desktop onto a fake VGA monitor (that doesn't exist) that is set to 2048x1152 in size, and set that fake desktop as "primary". That way, I could launch portal2.exe with "-w2048 -h1024 -sw" options and have it play at that resolution. It would otherwise clamp the resolution to the dimensions of the desktop. Of course, the game would be rendered on a monitor that does not exist, so I had to pass also the demo playback commands on the commandline (such as "+playdemo redracer2") and trust that it renders properly despite being completely unseen. I also had to edit splitscreen.txt in order to make the custom 2:1 aspect ratio work properly, without black borders.

Note: The avi option in "startmovie" is limited to 4 gigabytes in size, making it useless. That is why I had to use the silly tga files option.
_________
This video is part of my experiment series on making tool-assisted Portal 2 machinima/demonstration videos.
I believe it is possible to create interesting TAS-like videos in Portal 2. They are created by playing normally (albeit with a heavy slowdown using the "host_timescale" option) in co-op mode, and then replayed using either the split-screen mode or by having player 1 (Atlas) in full-screen. (Full-screening P-Body is not currently possible with the console commands that I know.)

One possibility is that Atlas is the sole owner of the camera. When that is the case, there are two possible art directions that I can envision.
-- Case 1: Atlas will be the "main" player, directing his own performance from a first-person perspective, and P-Body is a comic relief extra.
-- Case 2: Atlas will hold the camera, but P-Body is the main actor. The role of Atlas is to capture the P-Body's performance in the most entertaining manner, always striving to find the best possible camera angles.
In the split-screen mode (case 3), each actor (P-Body and Atlas) is their own director, responsible for making an entertaining performance and also of capturing each others from third-person perspective in the most entertaining way.
It is also possible to switch between these three styles at any point in the video.
No matter which mode, basic videographic principles are to be heeded: Keep the camera stable and always focused at something that is interesting somehow. At all times, provide the viewer a clear view to whatever is most interesting at the moment to see.

I created three videos, each demonstrating one of these cases.
-- Case 1: https://youtu.be/wTyMi5RAtHU [Atlas is the main player, P-Body is an extra].
-- Case 2: https://youtu.be/OIyjqz-Uq1Y [Atlas let's us see P-Body's performance]
-- Case 3: https://youtu.be/Dqggfqk-Zfo [Split-screen, each player is both an actor and a cameraman]
Note: Because I created each video playing by myself, and Portal 2 does not allow simultaneous input to both characters from one PC, the actors do not act completely independently.

snippet.title: Portal 2 Co-op solution for: mp_coop_paint_red_racer
snippet.description:
This video shows approximately how I and my friend first solved this stage of Portal 2 Co-operative challenge. I uploaded it, because from what I have seen, everyone solved this stage differently. One more solution cannot hurt.

(Quirky movements & execution in general is because I played this alone; both players were controlled by me in a high resolution time sharing manner. Oh, and I did not know of m_pitch2 command yet, so the mouse axis for players 1 and players 2 worked the opposite way.)

Also, I finally learned how to produce good quality videos from Portal 2, despite my hardware being quite low par (it's a GMA 4500M, which does not even support antialias).

Created with these commands in the development console:
ss_map mp_coop_paint_red_racer [In order to load a map in split-screen co-op mode]
ss_map mp_coop_paint_red_racer [Did twice because the first time would just terminate the single-player game session]
sv_cheats 1 [So that timescale works]
host_timescale 0.08 [This makes the game run at a much slower speed, allowing more precise movements]
BindToggle "z" in_forceuser [The z key is bound to switching players]
record redracer [Start recording movie]
stop [End recording]
host_timescale 1.0 [Reset to a normal speed]
host_framerate 240 [Set a fixed framerate for video recording]
startmovie test [Begin recording audio&video]
playdemo redracer [Playback the recorded demo]
ss_force_primary_fullscreen 1 [This puts player 1 in full screen]
endmovie [End recording audio&video]


I recorded this video at 1366x768, 240 fps into individual uncompressed TGA files. Because I quickly ran out of disk space that way (and with Source it is not possible to save to other location than the predefined one), I also ran in Cygwin a script which continually transferred the TGA files across network to another computer.
After recording, the tga files were combined into a single recording using a combination of scripts that also do the motion blurring by reducing into 30 fps with weighted average using a gaussian curve. The video was also upscaled to 2732x1536 using a lanczos filter, in order to enable the 1080p option in YouTube.
Note: The avi option in "startmovie" is limited to 4 gigabytes in size, making it useless.

snippet.title: Creating a YouTube video in QBasic
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video I will demonstrate how to use QBasic to create a video performance, something that an expensive tool like Microsoft Powerpoint is often used. It is useful when you need to generate lots of stuff programmatically. (This video is not entirely serious.)
This program will illustrate the anatomy of the standard 256-color VGA palette.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

This video also illustrates well the principle that in programming, it often happens that to achieve 2 minutes of glory, the amount of background work needed is way, way more than. The typing of this program takes several times longer than the time to watch its output, and that's with quite rapid typing.
And the unseen part, which is the designing of this program, testing the clarity of video and audio at each step, and the speech synthesis patch to DOSBox, took even much longer.

This video is PART 1. PART 2 (the produced video) can be seen here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-9QnckzyYvs

The background music is composed by me. I used the same music in my "Creating a snake game in QBasic" video, seen here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TUa5HJUebEA
However, in this video, I played it using my 2010 version of MIDINS, which means that the pitch slides and vibratos are heard properly as they should have been. In the other video, I used the 2000 version because the 2010 version did not exist yet.

In 2008, I created a Tool-Assisted Speedrun of Chrono Cross on the Playstation system, using pSX Linux version 1.13. It was not officially released on TASVideos, because it did not meet the site standard of reproducability (due to how it was made).
This is the first time I publish it in YouTube. I originally split it thematically into 27 parts, but YouTube's 15 minute upload limit requires me to publish it split into even more pieces.
This is part 27 of 52, or according to the original numbering, piece 1/2 of part 16/27.
The first part is here: https://youtu.be/LSVdQFVLvdU
The previous part (26, "The Einlazer") is here: https://youtu.be/6LI0Tv_dKL8
The next part (28, "The Grieving") is here: https://youtu.be/JUk6lpQ7eUo

Key events of this section: 
— Disassemble the Highwayman
— Explore the moment frozen in time
— Exposition by Miguel, by Crono, by Lucca and by Marle

Note: This is not an as-fast-as-possible game completion. While the playing precision is high, the speedrun employs a sort of sight-seeing route through the game.
More information: http://tasvideos.org/Bisqwit/Projects/ChronoCross.html
⌛ Total length of time played (including undone segments): ~26 hours.
⌚ Final playing time: 9 hours and 8 minutes and 25 seconds
✂ Total rerecord count: 47180
✄ Total segment count: 7959
Terminology: A speedrun with arbitrary segmentation (create & load save whenever you want) is called tool-assisted speedrun, or TAS for short. Many TASes do way more than that, but this movie does just that. The line between SDA speedruns and TASVideos speedruns is quite narrow. This falls in the between, not quite fitting either site.

Apologies about the bad video quality; I don't have better quality originals, and there is no input file with which to create a new dump from the emulator, as explained on the webpage for more information.
There is also an all-in-one-part video available at https://youtu.be/5LG9T4kbD64 . However, it is unfortunately of slightly even worse video quality.

snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video, I create an assembler program that plays back several favourite NES songs using only the 3-channel+noise PC speaker found in the Tandy 1000.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

A month ago I demonstrated the 3½-channel PC speaker of Tandy 1000. You can see and hear it in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e3L_Ceat4Ss
I wrote that example in GW-BASIC, but everyone was left hanging over the following problem: GW-BASIC has certain limits. You cannot reproduce fine vibrato of NES songs in it, because the PLAY statement is too coarse. You would have to do any serious music playing in the assembler language. What would a serious attempt sound like?
In this tool-assisted education video, I create, from scratch, an assembler program that plays back several favourite NES songs using only Tandy 1000 sound hardware.

Miscellania:
-- The OS that shows up in the beginning is Amiga Research Operating System, i.e. AROS for short. This is the first time that I feature an operating system that is fundamentally different from either Windows or Linux. (MS-DOS is not fundamentally different from Windows.)
-- The AROS desktop theme is the default one from the Icaros distribution. However, I used a custom 1232x700 resolution, enabled by hacking QEMU & BIOS.
-- The music that plays in the movie (before the assembler program is finished) is played back through 8bitbubsy's high quality Protracker clone. Protracker was a very popular music creation tool for the Amiga, used by professionals and amateurs alike. You can find more information about that project at: https://sourceforge.net/projects/protracker/
-- The two MODs that play here on Protracker are: Capslock by Mick Rippon, and Phoenix by Groo/CNCD. Both gentlemen were very generous and happy to permit me to use their music from the 1990s in this video. Thank you!
-- This movie was a lot more work than I expected to produce. I created the assembler program (SND player) in less than a day, but creating the video for it took weeks. Let's just say, encoding a video with all the alpha-blended overlays and temporal blurring at 4240x2400 resolution takes anything from 8 to 30 hours per pass. And I had to redo it more than ten times, because of all kinds of reasons. It was quite exhausting. Oh, and I also had to write the tools that enable me to do those video tricks in the first place. I still don't own any video editing software other than those which I have made.
-- The video resolution in the source code editing is 848x480. I crafted the display mode very carefully to make pixels look sharp in YouTube's 480p mode while it being a widescreen mode. However, the actual editor ran in 416x936 (52x59) mode. I changed it into a two-column 848x480 with video editing magic. While editing the source code, I paid careful attention to how it would appear in the two-column mode. I chose the two-column mode for two reasons: To maximize the amount of onscreen context while the code was being written in order to minimize the disorientation when following the video; and to most effectively utilize the widescreen video area that I wanted to indeed use.
-- The video resolution while the SND player runs is 320x200. This is the standard CGA 40x25 text mode.
-- The video uploaded to YouTube had 4240x2400 resolution. As usual, I did all processing at this resolution. You can verify this by displaying the video in "Original" mode. At that resolution, the Protracker overlay is clearly readable at all times (assuming your display device supports that kind of resolution!), even when it's reduced into a small stamp in the corner of the editing window.
-- Please disregard the PT overlay that shows at 8:25 to 8:31. It was a postprocessing error. Considering the long time it took to encode the video each time, I was not looking forward to one more encoding pass and I let that error slip.
-- Because the code featured in this video was the longest so far of my videos, yet I had half the normal time to create it, I had to tweak my editing process to include new editing techniques that reduce the amount of typing. See if you can spot them. (Remind you, this is a tool-assisted education video. Even my editing is tool-assisted.) I also had to speed up the typing a bit, as well.

Drats, I think I hit YouTube's movie description length limit. More information (and source code) at: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/tandysnd.html

snippet.title: Featuring: Javascript PC emulator by Fabrice Bellard
snippet.description:
Javascript PC emulator can run Linux (JSLinux) within the web browser. Yes, it is real, actual Linux kernel. With busybox + ucLibc + tcc.

I discovered of this project just today, and within 4 hours I had a video ready for upload, while I am still working on another video.
In this video, I simply showcase JSLinux. I show how to compile a program within it, using mr. Bellard's TCC.
The program that I wrote* for this video simply calculates a continued fraction for a given real number.  For example, it can tell you that 1.766666666666667 (this video's aspect ratio) looks like 53/30. It is useful when you need to find a fractional approximation for a value. It occurs in programming and in video processing once in a while.

JSLinux web page: http://bellard.org/jslinux/

Fabrice Bellard is one programmer whom I can humbly admire. His accomplishments are significant and well known. He is the principal author of QEmu and ffmpeg, two very important and well known open source projects, but he also is an IOCCC [International Obfuscated C Code Contest] winner for two separate occassions, and held the world record for most computed digits of pi for a time. I learned of him the first time in the 1990s when I was studying the workings of LZEXE, which he wrote.
You can find more about mr. Bellard here: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrice_Bellard
IOCCC is an interesting contest I fondly follow (at its own pace). More about it here: http://www.ioccc.org/

In this video also appears William Shubert's KGS [KGS Go Server] client "cgoban3". I sometimes play Go on KGS, though moreoften I just watch. If you are a beginner at Go and you are friendly, I may gladly help you. KGS homepage: http://www.gokgs.com/ Introduction to Go: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/go2.html

The soundtrack in this video is an SPC to MIDI to OPL3 conversion of the song "Boy Meets Girl" from Earthbound, a well known SNES game. Mr. Bellard was not an author of that game. For some reason, the music does not appear to be perfectly in tune. I apologize. You can see the workflow of my SPC...OPL3 conversions in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7IeO7CYFd9E&feature=related

The desktop background image is a screenshot from the Hikaru no Go anime, cropped, scaled into 424x240, quantized and dithered using animmerger, and then upscaled into 848x480. Animmerger is one of my creations and is available at: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/animmerger.html
This desktop is not my primary one. It is entirely made as a set piece for YouTube videos. The desktop was rendered through Xephyr and OpenSSH tunnelling to a Cygwin X11 desktop, running on Windows 7. There were actually more layers of systems than appears in the video. The video was recorded with CamStudio recorder v2.6.

*) The continued fractions program was actually written originally by Juhana Sadeharju. I did some small changes into it, such as changing any Finnish text in it into English.

P.S. If you are curious to see for yourself what the well known command of doom, "rm -rf /", does, now you can do it perfectly safely with JSLinux. Mr. rbochet demonstrates it here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9g6gbw3NpKY&feature=related

snippet.title: Super Mario Bros 3: Remastered Audio Experiment
snippet.description:
Fooling around. Music replaced by me, with more modern Mario music. Sound effects intact.
Created in 2007 for http://tasvideos.org/.
It was an entertaining challenge.
Apologies about the bad video quality; I have lost the original video material and had to settle transcoding a less-optimal quality video.
I did not compose the music. The music comes from mostly from Super Mario Galaxy and/or Super Mario All Stars.
I hacked the game ROM to disregard playing music, thus playing only sound effects; and I made the emulator log into file whenever the game _wants_ to change music. Then I used the log in conjunction with a script I made to mix mp3 music tracks with the game's audio.

The interlacing comes from using a filter in MEncoder that converts 60 fps into 30 fps with even and odd fields. At that time I considered it a better alternative than to coldly drop 50% of frames, seeing as how YouTube clamps the framerate at 30.

snippet.title: Portal: WDYM You trapped yourself AGAIN? [PART 1/2]
snippet.description:
This is a collection of various ways to get GLaDOS to notice you've trapped yourself in Portal. (With occasional false positives and false negatives.)

I like the sequel, Portal 2, but one thing I felt that the game was a disappointment compared to the original Portal was that they failed to follow the rule "The Dev Team Thinks of Everything". In Portal 2, the chambers in which you can achieve a you-trapped-yourself message are far fewer than those in Portal 1.

Below is the list of showcased trappings. Indicated is whether GLaDOS notices you are trapped, whether you are truly trapped until GLaDOS notices your situation, and the method of trapping.

PART 1:
-- Chamber 1: [GLaDOS: No] [Trap: Yes] [Method: Physics]

-- Chamber 4: [GLaDOS: Yes] [Trap: Yes] [Method: Glitch]
-- Chamber 5: [GLaDOS: Yes] [Trap: No] Does this count? [Method: Portal]
-- Chamber 5: [GLaDOS: Yes] [Trap: Yes] [Method: Physics]

-- Chamber 8: [GLaDOS: Yes] [Trap: Yes] Does this count? [Method: Portal]
-- Chamber 8: [GLaDOS: No] [Trap: Yes] At least now I'm trapped. [Method: Glitch]

-- Chamber 12: [GLaDOS: Yes] [Trap: Yes] [Method: Portal]

snippet.title: OpenGL scene in truecolor
snippet.description:
This is a follow-up to the OpenGL programming example posted earlier.

It contains the same scene as in https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vkUwT9U1GzA , but now rendered in truecolor, with motion blur, in 3200x2400 resolution (so yes, this is really HD). Still with OSMesa, still with 99% the same program. I changed the PC::W and PC::H constants and changed PC::Render() to save the contents of PC::ImageBuffer[] into a file each frame. And I first rendered the whole thing with lightweight settings, moved around and saved all movements into a file. Then I changed the settings to those large-resolution ones and changed the program to load all movements from that file rather than from the keyboard and the mouse, so it replicates all my actions smoothly even while it's running at about 1 fps (or less, due to motion blurring and lzopping).

The NTSC effect on the QBASIC window in which I type the message was intentionally produced as a stark contrast to the clinical high quality in the scene that follows. I actually meant to vary the saturation a lot more and do other gimmics related to bad TV transmission, but I couldn't get them right and looking good. The combination of bad video quality and an eerie music was aiming to produce an impression of a transmission from a parallel reality. The eerie part subsides gradually as the message becomes clear, having resolved completely when the actual 3D video begins. In the 3D video, some instruments of the music (which is the same as in the original OpenGL programming example video) have been octave-downshifted to produce a "different, but also the same" type of effect. I play exactly one loop of the song, and produce an end into it with Audacity magic. The ending of the video was not as precisely timed to the song's end as I hoped it would be by chance.

- Hudmaker (This converts raw audio and video streams and overlays graphical items, like subtitles, into it, and sends result to encoder)
- Tile4 (This did the four-video inset at the end of the video. I got the idea from Freddy Wong (user:Freddiew).)

snippet.title: Portal 2 foolery: Portal Bump still works. [chapter 3]
snippet.description:
In this video I use a technique that is very familiar to certain people who have played Portal 1, and demonstrate that it still works in Portal 2, although the places where it can be used are far fewer. Also, they apparently put a clip-brush around all observation rooms, preventing the _player_ from entering there, but no such restriction exists for objects. I find it sad that they chose this approach in level design. There are many jackhammer design resolutions in Portal 2, for things that should be solved by better design. (Instant kill zones and clipbrushes for areas that are clearly easy to enter, but are just not what the plot calls for; sometimes even plot-cued exceptions to portalability disregarding visual cues. Some corridors have clip brushes for items, preventing boxes being dragged through them, even if the player can simply walk through and there's no emancipation field. In Portal 1 they embraced players creating their own creative solutions; in Portal 2 it appears like some manager decided that railroading is a prime directive. Lead the flock on the plot-directed course, prod harshly anyone who strays.)
Apologies about the bad video quality; I'm new to this.

snippet.title: Rockman Basics - WIP and walkthrough
snippet.description:
In 2005 I began creating a Rockman hack; that is, a custom game based on NES Mega Man's engine. Back then, I was among the few foremost experts on Mega Man game glitches in the world. (Well, I still am, but there now are a few people who know even more about them than I do.)
The basic principle of this hack was: Create a game that is impossible to complete without intrinsic knowledge about Mega Man glitches, but as much as possible in a teaching-learning manner, i.e. it should be fun and insightful to play. And it should be beautiful, as well, following the original style of art where possible.
Turns out those goals were rather difficult to implement. The hack is still unfinished; in fact, just three and half stages are done.

When I recorded this video, it had been more than a year since I last touched this game. I wanted to show an intuitive "first experience" to the game, with a voiceover narration explaining some concepts, while also making sure to walk through all existing content so far.
But turns out that unlike some people like Transgenic86, I am awfully bad at doing voiceovers, so here you will only see the playing part, but you will not get the voiceover part. I will try to add some relevant things as subtitles/annotations later.

Technical bits: Background art (trees, windows, electric wires etc.) were generated procedurally. Foreground art was also generated procedurally; in the level editor, platforms and overall layout of the levels are sketched entirely IN TEXT. Items, enemies are placed manually (as text).

Oh, and the video here is rendered in POV-Ray, versions 3.7.0 beta41..RC2. I almost forgot to mention it.
Apologies about the low resolution. The number of frames was high (59643), and even with 17 CPU cores at disposal, it still took two weeks to do the 3D rendering. Using a higher resolution would have made it even slower.
Antialias and radiosity were used. I also tried photons (for the glasses), but for some reasons POV-Ray would not honor my "photons { pass_through }" declaration. I wanted a pass_through without noshadow, but POV-Ray was no-go instead. The NES screen was processed with Blargg's NTSC filter, and I used tinterlace to halve the FPS rate for Youtube.

More information:
-- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/rockmanbasics/ (Web page of the hack)
-- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/rockedit.html (Source code of the level editor used; most surprisingly it is entirely ungraphical).

My recording of this video was originally 16:40 long, but thanks to the 15-minute limit Youtube recently reintroduced into my account, I had to cut the video short.

snippet.title: 256 colors is enough for everyone
snippet.description:
In this video I use source code as means to illustrate how stunning RGB graphics can be achieved on a 256-color screen, so much that you actually may doubt whether it is really only 256 colors.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

Note: The animation does not look blurry because of dithering. Dithering does increase blurriness a little, but in a different way and most certainly not this much. The reason to blurriness is that the actual video is all about orbs that do not have a defined edge (they're just clouds of pure light). And then there's motion blur that is added to it. In other words, the _original_ video material is blurry. I created it this way to maximize the number of color mixtures shown.

[SPOILERS BELOW]
Disclaimer: The story behind this video is a fabrication to justify the fact that the code is too complex for QuickBASIC to run, and too heavy for today's computers even if translated to C, unless run on a multicore CPU. All the technical details are absolutely correct. I did indeed write the first revisions of this program in QB, but I then translated it to C++,  with which I created the actual animations after refining the code a bit, and I backported the changes to QB to show how it _would_ be done, did QB not have those limits. The reason why it is slow is not because of dithering, but because of the really ineffective algorithm for rendering stars, dithering or not; what with doing some 25000 distance calculations tests _per pixel_.
[END SPOILERS]

Also, I am not advocating anyone to replace 24bpp with 8bpp. Rather, I am trying to educate programmers to utilize paletted resources better, and I illustrate some exact algorithms with which to achieve that. Stop using floyd-steinberg for GIF animations!
If you cannot get the program working, you are not yet part of the target audience.

Note: In this video, I used a copy of actual QuickBASIC 4.5 by Microsoft... well, Megasoft Corp. However, after creating and publishing this video, I discovered QB64, a modern free port of QB. I ported this program to QB64! It works, though minor changes. Here is a link to the QB64 version's source code: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/sfield_qb64.bas
Note that it still requires computers from a parallel universe to run smoothly...

snippet.title: QuickBASIC realtime SGF replayer. 囲碁: Redrose [1p] vs. Tartrate [PART 3/3]
snippet.description:
2003年の囲碁回戦。対局者：白― ロシヤからの初段のプロシクシナ・スヴェトラナ、黒―タルトレートと呼ばれる不思議な挑戦者(負けなし)。場所：ＫＧＳ。批評は英語。リプレイ：私が作ったのＢＡＳＩＣプログラム。Somehow, Youtube revoked my privilege to upload longer than 15 minute movies, without warning, without message, after already granting me that once, similarly without any announcement or rationale. Oh well. Back to multipart videos then :(
Due to this unexpected constraint however, I will not publish here the video in which I create the program (for it is considerably longer than 15 minutes); I will just link to the source code, here: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/qbsgf.html

Anyway, in this video, I showcase a QuickBASIC program that I just created. It reads and parses a SGF file, which is a file that can store a recording of a number of board game sessions, including my favourite, the game of Go. The SGF file encodes a tree in ASCII format with branches and where each branch has a lists of moves, where each move can have a number of arbitrary attributes attached to it, such as comments. The different branches convey variations in the game.
The SGF file replayer not only parses the SGF file, but replays it as if it happened in real time, displaying spectators' comments along with the moves.

To demonstrate the program, I chose one of my favourite games from KGS archives. Tartrate is a legendary Go player, whose identity is still a mystery, who appeared on the KGS Go Server in the 2003. He has been sometimes likened to Sai from the Hikaru no Go anime. When this game was played, he had already established a lossless track record against many of the strongest amateurs on the KGS. He had never been defeated. This one time I happened to be lucky and observe him play a professional Go player, Svetlana Šikšina from Russia. They are both incredibly strong players. In this game, Tartrate begins the game using a very inconventional opening. These factors gave this game truly an instant classic status.
Note: Players commenting on this game have obviously become often a lot stronger and often a lot smarter since this game was played (2003). Their comments are only shown here as citations, as part of the back-then original game observing performance, replayed by this program of mine.

There are some people who think that the audience should be completely silent (even going as far as hiding the kibitz window) while the game is in progress, and of course I am not fan of the "what's in your fridge" style chat that goes on during the game, but I think in general, the kibitz is an integral part of the entertainment of watching the match, and often provides useful insight to the game, as long as the topic is about the game. The suspense and waiting for what's coming next (though one can only guess) is a significant factor in the entertainment. It is not nearly as entertaining to watch the game if you can simply click forward one move at time at your own pace. This is why I made this program play the game at its original pace. Apologies for the fact that ko are not indicated; I fixed that in the next version.

snippet.title: AdLib "speech synthesis": Joona
snippet.description:
AdLib "speech synthesis" test. I did this in 1999.

THIS IS JUST A QUICK PROOF OF CONCEPT; IT IS NOT A SAMPLE OF REFINED TECHNOLOGY. In fact, it is barely intelligible. If you don't know the text beforehand, you likely cannot understand it. This program is reading the Biblical book of Jonah in Finnish language.

TÄMÄ ON VAIN PIKAINEN KOE; EI MIKÄÄN KEHITTYNEEN TEKNOLOGIAN NÄYTE. Ja tosiaankin siitä ei juurikaan saa selvää, etenkään jos teksti ei ole ennestään tuttua. Tietokoneohjelma lukee ääneen Joonan kirjaa suomenkielisestä Raamatusta.

I used Scream Tracker 3 to try and create AdLib samples that most closely sounded like each phoneme in my opinion (vowels and consonants), and I wrote a C++ program to play those samples according to the text.
With Finnish language, text-to-speech is relatively easy because it has nearly a 1-to-1 correspondance between letters and phonemes, unlike some other languages like English. Indeed, it is one of the reasons why native Finns find it very difficult to learn fluent English pronounciation. (There are other reasons too.)

In Finnish language, there are eight vowels: A, E, I, O, U, Y, Ä and Ö. There are only a few consonants: D, H, J, K, L, M, N, NG, P, R, S, T and V. In addition to those, foreign consonants such as B, F, G, Š (SH) and W are recognized and variably pronounced "right", depending on the speaker. Often they are aliased to the native consonants P, V, K, S and V, respectively. In some dialects, D is also aliased to T or R. Each native letter corresponds to a single phoneme with a distinct sound and they always sound approximately the same regardless of their position in a word, meaning e.g. that the words "kansio" and "oksain" are true anagrams in the sense that you could take the audio recording of one word, split into pieces and concatenate after rearranging the pieces and thus produce the other word (with only minor glitches). In English, if you take the recording of the word "friend", you cannot splice+combine it to sound like "finder", or similarly the word "masculine" into "alien scum".

snippet.title: Doom on CGA (monochrome), 16-color EGA and the NES
snippet.description:
This video illustrates running the PC game Doom on the CGA, EGA and NES displays*. It is a continuation to this video that I uploaded previously: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9YoqUM1ZLQ0

The different display modes featured in this video are listed below.
-- 1: CGA monochrome 640x200 mode (QBASIC's SCREEN 2) on a RGB display. There are exactly two colors: Black and White. One of the colors could be changed to any of the standard 16 CGA colors (for the entire screen at once), but I chose to stick with white.
-- 2: EGA 640x350 16-color mode (QBASIC's SCREEN 9). Palette was hand-chosen from the 64-color available selection on the EGA.
-- 3: Nintendo Entertainment System. Uses 256x224 display, divided into 16x16 tiles, each being a 2-bit bitmap + a 2-bit index to a list of palettes. A total of 4 palettes per screen, each palette being 3-color + one global background color (black here). Basically 13 colors were chosen from the NES's available 53 colors. Sprites were not utilized. Technically, this would be possible to do on the NES, except for the fact that the NES PPU's memory is not nearly fast enough to update the screen this fast. Maybe if you had a cartridge with a custom mapper that remaps VROM instantaneously so all you'll have to do is update the attribute tables once per frame. But then there's also the per-screen limit of unique tiles (tile number), which is not addressed in this video.

I am positively surprised how good each of these turned out, especially the EGA one. Doom would have been totally playable on the EGA! Marginally playable also on the CGA. Handhelds designers, take note!

* Or rather, it is a recording of shareware Doom being played on VGA mode 13h earlier, that I postprocessed to conform to the hardware constraints of each output device. It contains the same video clip three times, rendered with different color features. It is NOT a palette hack on 256-color Doom; no extra WADs or TSRs were loaded.

All the colorization, quantization and dithering was done with animmerger, https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/animmerger.html
I used positional dithering, because it is very well suited for animation, and because I like its appearance. Non-positional error-diffusion dithering methods, such as floyd-steinberg, produce massive amounts of *jittering* garbage.

One thing which I wanted to do, but I don't have the technology for it yet, is that I wanted to make the music & sound in the NES section sound like it would actually be on the NES. That is, two square wave channels, one triangle wave, one noise generator and one DPCM channel is all you get. But doing this would have delayed this video probably indefinitely; I've been wanting this for years so far but I have yet to make a breakthrough. I also contemplated on transforming the sound like it comes through the PC speaker (using the 6-bit PCM PIT trick) and using that in the CGA sections (I've tested similar conversions earlier successfully), but somehow I didn't feel it is necessary.

P.S. I think Doom's sound effects, especially the monster sounds, are awesome.

Here is the explanation of new the original dithering algorithm that I use in this video: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/story/howto/dither/jy/

snippet.title: Doom on CGA (4-color and composite/colorburst mode) and EGA
snippet.description:
This video illustrates running the PC game Doom on the CGA* display.
See also part 2 (CGA monochrome, EGA hires and the NES) at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Nz_QB26Clw

The CGA, as featured on original PCs, is capable of two graphical display modes:
320x200 4-color mode and a 640x200 monochrome mode. This page lists all the details of how the colors can be selected in those modes: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_8-bit_computer_hardware_palettes#CGA

The different display modes featured in this video are listed below. The first three of them are the same as QBASIC's SCREEN 1, but with different palette selections:
-- 1: CGA palette 0 in Low intensity setting: Black, Red, Green, Yellow.
-- 2: CGA palette 1 in Low intensity setting: Black, Cyan, Magenta, White. (Almost as useful as monochrome!)
-- 3: CGA palette 2 in Low intensity setting and Background color changed: BLUE, Cyan, Red, White.
-- 4: CGA monochrome 640x200 mode (QBASIC's SCREEN 2) on Composite Color Display. All colors are colorburst *artifacts* arising from deliberately chosen monochrome pixel patterns, yielding a color resolution of 160x200. The rendering algorithm was copied from DOSBox-0.74; I don't know whether it is accurate or not.
-- 5: EGA 320x200 16-color mode (QBASIC's SCREEN 7). Provided for comparison.
-- 6: 16 arbitrarily chosen colors (with NeuQuant algorithm, sadly it seemed to neglect blue tones completely).

Range-compensated = Input colors were linearly scaled from the 00..FFh range to a 00..AAh range to better match the range of normal-intensity CGA palette. The proportion of black in the scene also increases as a side effect.
Artificially colored = Means nothing. During the production I tried to tone dark input colors towards blue to better utilize the palette features, but as I developed the color comparison function further, I found this step unnecessary.

* Or rather, it is a recording of shareware Doom being played on VGA mode 13h earlier, that I postprocessed to conform to the hardware constraints of the CGA. It contains the same video clip six times, rendered with different color features. It is NOT a palette hack on 256-color Doom; no extra WADs or TSRs were loaded.

All the colorization, quantization and dithering was done with animmerger, https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/animmerger.html
I used positional dithering, because it is very well suited for animation, and because I like its appearance. Non-positional error-diffusion dithering methods, such as floyd-steinberg, produce massive amounts of *jittering* garbage.

P.S. I think Doom's sound effects, especially the monster sounds, are awesome.

Here is the explanation of new the original dithering algorithm that I use in this video: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/story/howto/dither/jy/

snippet.title: MBROLA song: Solomon's Key
snippet.description:
MBROLA song: Solomon's Key

This series is a proof-of-concept experiment on using MBROLA as a vocaloid.

How it is made:

First, an emulator is run so that audio is produced. The emulator runs e.g. Solomon's Key on the NES, or a NSF dump thereof. The emulator will log the audio output into a "SND" file which only contains information about pitch & volume for each signal generator, 60 times per second. (iNES 5.0 is an example of such emulator, but I used something other.)

Then a program is run that reads the SND file, and translates the signal generator parameters into notes that have a start-time, duration and pitch. Said notes are converted into a stream of phonemes, that are saved into a .pho file. Four such files are generated, one for each channel of the NES. I wrote this program in PHP.

Then those .pho files are converted into .wav files by the MBROLA speech synthesizer. A maximum of four wav files, one for each simultaneous voice.

Finally, the .wav files are mixed together with SoX to produce what you hear here.

Naturally, it is much easier (less laborsome) to combine an existing stream of pitches with an algorithm that serializes random phonemes, than to type vocals that actually make sense and to time them correctly with a melody. snippet.title: POV-Ray animation "Descent, level 1" [Test encoding 2]
snippet.description:
I rendered Descent level 1 using POV-Ray, using the original map data and graphics from the game, and a program I created for converting the game data into a POV-Ray script. I added bloom and HDRI tone-mapping in post-process.
The camera navigates the tunnels completely automatically; I programmed a navigator, but not a route.
The music is also from the game; it is a MIDI played through a OPL3 synthesizer.

There are some errors in textures; some of them are transparent when they should not be, and there are no animating textures, and some UV vectors are plain wrong. Apologies. Especially the UV vectors were difficult to correct to even this degree.

The animation was rendered at an intended 45 fps playback rate, at 1920x1080 resolution. However, Youtube maxes at 30 fps, so I first changed it to 60 fps through frame duplication, and then reduced to 30 fps by a "tinterlace" filter which halves the fps to 30, while doubling the resolution to 1920x2160. I had to redo that encoding numerous times, because MEncoder consistently kept crashing at around 4-minute mark. This very video was also cut short through a crash; it should have been more than 8 minutes. Oh well. Good enough, here goes.

snippet.title: ADLMIDI: Free MIDI player with OPL3 emulation & reverb
snippet.description:
This video demonstrates some key features of an open-source/free MIDI player that I developed, including multiple OPL3 card emulation, four-operator instruments, automatic arpeggio to relieve congestion (in this video, tuned to be overaggressive for artistic reasons) and a built-in reverb filter.
Link: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/adlmidi.html

It is a console program that runs on POSIX and Win32 systems, and here you see it being run in DOSBox with the aid of HX, a DOS extender that provides a Win32-compatible API. There were some difficulties here and there but they were mostly solved. (For instance, I had to record the audio separately on Win32 because it was chopping too much on DOS.)

The video was recorded in an EGA display mode (350 scanlines rather than the normal VGA 400 scanlines), and further postprocessed by adding scanlines, by adding a faux HAM/color leak filter and by blooming the highlights a bit, for artistic reasons alone.

You can find a precompiled 32-bit Windows binary of ADLMIDI here: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/src/adlmidi-122-win32.zip

snippet.title: Ancient machine (POV-Ray animation, HD & HDRI)
snippet.description:
This is a visual inspiration about a music soundtrack in Final Fantasy V. I did not add any sound effects; the audio is verbatim from the game's background music.

I modelled and rendered this using POV-Ray, postprocessed using EXR-Utils and PFSTools, in particular using the pfstmo_fattal02 tone-mapping tool. (It is also responsible for the unfortunately pronounced moiré effects on the background).

Originally designed in 2002, refined in 2010. Particles calculated with ODE.

I began this modelling by creating a mathematical map of the music, listing the periodicity of each element of the sound with regards to a global timer (the big pounding sound). Then I translated each periodicity element into a POV-Ray function, and used that function to animate the corresponding visual element in the animation.

Also, it took 7 attempts for me to re-encode and re-upload this video before Youtube finally got it right. Previous encodes were outright rejected (unable to process) or were published at wrong aspect ratio.

I rendered this video at the resolution 1440x1080, 60 fps. Using MEncoder's "tinterlace" filter, the fps was dropped to 30 while the resolution was doubled to 1440x2160 (because Youtube caps fps at 30. This also introduced a motion blur effect). However, when I uploaded this video (after multiple failures), Youtube ignored the aspect ratio setting (4:3) from the stream headers and instead determined it from the resolution (2:3). So I had to double the resolution again, making it 2880x2160 using a Lanczos filter.

The final encode, the one finally accepted by Youtube, was encoded to H.264 format overnight using the following parameters: crf=22:rc_lookahead=32:frameref=15:trellis=2:me=umh:me_range=64
:subq=10:partitions=all:fullrange=on:subme=10:bframes=0:threads=4
This produced a 575 MB MKV for this 111 seconds long video.

snippet.title: Creating a MIDI player in MS-DOS / BASIC
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video, I demonstrate how to write a MIDI player from scratch.

Please see this page for more details, including the source code:
https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/midiplay.html

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

MIDI is a Music Interchange file format which describes music in abstract terms such as "piano key C-4 pressed down". A synthesizer is required to reproduce audible music from MIDI files. In this tool-assisted education video, I create one such synthesizer program from scratch, using the OPL3 hardware synthesizer as the backend for generating the actual sounds.

You see me type every line. The resulting program contains the rudimentary features for playing most MIDI files just fine, including the pitch slides and pans, but it lacks other special effects like vibrato, nor does it support any more tunings than the standard equal-interval mathematical tuning. It supports the loopStart/loopEnd mechanism found in authentic Final Fantasy VII MIDI files.

This is probably my best MS-DOS MIDI player so far (at least in some aspects), and I have written two. The first one, written in 1998, however eventually evolved also to convert them into S3Ms...
This was also the most difficult production-for-show so far in terms of getting it right; BASIC has its own unique challenges at debugging it, and I did accidentally introduce many bugs into this program, despite writing it from a script. I did fix them too, though. But more time was consumed doing that than I had planned.

Music played during this video:
- Zoolook by Jogeir Liljedalh (a few seconds in the beginning)
- Predicament / Chrono Cross (BGM during programming)
- Chmmr and Arilou themes / Star Control III (MIDI)
- Barret and battle themes / Final Fantasy VII (MIDI)
- Airship and Big whale themes / Final Fantasy IV (MIDI, sequenced by Andrew Thompson)

Songs begin at:
12:00 FF4 Airship
13:02 FF7 Barret
14:33 SC3 Arilou
15:56 FF7 Battle
17:27 FF4 Big Whale

My favourite part of this video: 08:53 onwards.

P.S. Eventually this program evolved into a C++ opensource project! Check it out here: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/source/adlmidi.html

snippet.title: POV-Ray animation "Dropping capsules" [HDRI Version]
snippet.description:
Physics engines are fascinating. Here, I tried out Open Dynamics Engine, ODE, and created this animation from the results of a simulation I created. It is my first program ever to use a serious physics engine. It is rendered using POV-Ray, an open source raytracing program.

I rendered this animation actually in three varieties:
- "SmoothTime Version", which has a high number of frames that are blurred together to produce a smooth, realistic animation. It is, however, rendered at a low resolution. Available here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIQ_4hnHZuM
- "HiRes Version", which was rendered at a high resolution. It has, however, a lower number of frames, which means that the animation appears more jerky and artificial, though it is very sharp. Available here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69G5kTbhZeM
- "HDRI Version", (THIS VIDEO). In which graphical details from both bright and dim areas are shown in the same frame by retouching each frame with a "tonemapping" algorithm. Additionally, this version is both high resolution and uses motion blur. There's really not that much "HDR" to do after all...

The video has no sound. I originally planned to add sounds -- the simulation program does indeed record all collisions that could produce sound -- but I have not yet figured out what would be the best way to actually produce the soundtrack.

ODE can be found at http://www.ode.org/ . POV-Ray can be found at http://www.povray.org/ .

P.S. The animation was originally supposed to feature coins that are dropped from a tall height. However, currently ODE lacks the code to calculate cylinder-cylinder collisions, which is why I had to change them into capsules. Interestingly enough, it is apparently easier to calculate capsule-capsule collisions.

Trivia: The animation contains 3000 capsules. snippet.title: Bisqwit's Duke Nukem 3D Deathmatch Map 010
snippet.description:
A deathmatch map I designed for Duke Nukem 3D once upon a time, somewhere between 1996 and 2001, exact timespan unknown.
In this video, I walk through the map, trying to discover&introduce all of its secrets.

Artistic disclaimer: It is not very professional looking: Back in the day, I didn't pay much attention to details like interesting/realistic lighting/shadows; instead, I was more fascinated with the quirks of Duke Nukem 3D's spatial model. Nevertheless, it was a fun map to play. Note: I had never watched Doctor Who, so I did not know about the TARDIS. There are only a few enemies, because 1) this was a deathmatch map, intended for player-versus-player battles and 2) I had no particular interest towards shoot-maim-and-kill paradigm at all; I was far more interested about spatial architecting.

Player disclaimer note: Recorded in DOSBox at 800x600 resolution (the maximum supported by Duke3D). It lagged seriously (on the AthlonXP 2400+), making it really difficult to control, which is why my controls appear rather jerky and rushed; inaccurate too. Also, Duke3D was not designed to have mouse Y axis configured for vertical aiming (the standard in Half-Life descendants). It was possible, but it had to be done in "digital" mode, which means it was very inaccurate and worked in jerky increments.

Time usage note: Due to the aforementioned lag, what appears like 10 seconds to you was really like 2 minutes to me. No exaggeration. This is why I don't stop long for any detail... The video took hours to record, after which I spent a few days tweaking the re-encoding parameters, after which the computer spent a few hours postprocessing the AVI recording, after which computers spent a few hours transferring data across the Internet, after which Youtube spent a few hours processing the video.

Video technical note: Recorded in a video mode that normally runs at 70.167 FPS. However, I hacked DOSBox to upscale the FPS by a factor of 3, meaning that the game experienced a video mode that refreshes the screen at 210.503 FPS. Then, my custom AVI recorder in DOSBox did a framerate reduction by a factor of 4 with weighted temporal averaging, resulting in an AVI that has a FPS of 52.62575.
This AVI was upscaled to 60.000 FPS with frame duplication (mencoder -ofps 60), and then reduced to 30.000 FPS with temporal interlacing filter (mencoder -vf tinterlace), to achieve the maximal content density for Youtube publication (Youtube caps framerate at 30.000, silently discarding anything above that). The video resolution was also changed to 1600x600 before tinterlace by doubling it horizontally, and tinterlace doubled it vertically to 1600x1200. This was uploaded to Youtube. Scenes that were in other resolution than 800x600 (such as 640x480 in Build and 640x400 in text mode) were crudely pixel-scaled to 800x600. It looks very ugly, but it contributes a very minor proportion to the video's length so I did not invest effort in that part (it would have been complicated to add a Lanczos rescaler to it due to working with 8-bit paletted graphics data). Audio was recorded at 48 kHz stereo and Duke3D was configured to use Gravis Ultrasound for both SFX and music. I reasoned that Gravis emulation would give the best proportion of sound quality versus CPU usage within the emulated system.

Link: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/kala/jhm010-map.zip

snippet.title: POV-Ray animation "Dropping capsules" [HiRes Version]
snippet.description:
Physics engines are fascinating. Here, I tried out Open Dynamics Engine, ODE, and created this animation from the results of a simulation I created. It is my first program ever to use a serious physics engine. It is rendered using POV-Ray, an open source raytracing program.

I rendered this animation actually in three varieties:
- "SmoothTime Version", which has a high number of frames that are blurred together to produce a smooth, realistic animation. It is, however, rendered at a low resolution. Available here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIQ_4hnHZuM
- "HiRes Version", (THIS VIDEO), which was rendered at a high resolution. It has, however, a lower number of frames, which means that the animation appears more jerky and artificial, though it is very sharp.
- "HDRI Version", in which graphical details from both bright and dim areas are shown in the same frame by retouching each frame with a "tonemapping" algorithm. Additionally, this version is both high resolution and uses motion blur. There's really not that much "HDR" to do after all... Available here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3sjHsmicDqU

The video has no sound. I originally planned to add sounds -- the simulation program does indeed record all collisions that could produce sound -- but I have not yet figured out what would be the best way to actually produce the soundtrack.

ODE can be found at http://www.ode.org/ . POV-Ray can be found at http://www.povray.org/ .

P.S. The animation was originally supposed to feature coins that are dropped from a tall height. However, currently ODE lacks the code to calculate cylinder-cylinder collisions, which is why I had to change them into capsules. Interestingly enough, it is apparently easier to calculate capsule-capsule collisions.

Trivia: The animation contains 3000 capsules. In addition, because the rendering also shows some "walls" and "lamps" that are on the floor, I had to introduce them, too, to ODE, so that the capsules will properly not-intersect with them. In total, the simulation thus contains 3010 objects, and it runs for 7000 frames (of which 1170 are rendered in the "high resolution version"). The simulation data took about 6 hours to calculate (non threading). The "high resolution" version took about 19 hours to render. It includes the "radiosity" and "antialias" features of POV-Ray, both of which significantly increase the rendering time. The POV-Ray scene contains 5 regular light_source declarations. (All light comes from the bulbs that are seen in the scene.)

Produced in June 2010, uploaded in November 2010.

snippet.title: 3D antialias illustration
snippet.description:
This video illustrates the importance of antialiasing in 3D content.
This video has the same 14-second scene rendered 4 times with different settings each time. Pay attention to the annotations.

It is rendered with POV-Ray, but the technique is similar to mipmapping / anisotropic filtering found in 3D display cards.

The video size is 320x240, but I upsampled it with a Lanzos filter to prevent Youtube from reducing the quality too much. There is no audio.

The texture is a wooden plank texture from iStockPhoto.

Explanation of the aliasing effect (and especially the moiré effect): When high-contrast, high resolution graphics are displayed on a low-resolution display, it is not easy to decide how each pixel is to be colored.
Imagine that you have a cross-ruled paper with just a 5x5 grid on it: 5 cells down, 5 cells across. For the sake of exercise, you want to draw a 8x8 checkerboard (as in chess). Each cell of the grid must be completely filled with just one color. How would you do it? It impossible to draw 32 white cells and 32 black cells (of the checkerboard), for your paper grid only contains 25 cells in total. (Analogy: The video game screen contains only 320x240 pixels in total. Each pixel can contain only one color tone at a given time.) The likely end result will be, that you have some cells randomly colored white and others black.
Now, imagine you will have to rotate the checkerboard a bit (say, 20 degrees), and draw it again. What will the result be? Probably the same, except some white cells have changed to black and vice versa. Repeat this process 10 times, and animate the 5x5 grids you have produced, and you've got a full-blown Moiré effect at your hands.
This is because you've done "aliasing": You have decided that each cell has a 1-1 correspondance to _some_ cell in the original checkerboard.
However, if you were to superimpose the 5x5 grid on top of the 8x8 grid, you would notice that each 5x5 grid cell actually coincides with a number of distinct 8x8 grid cells. In fact, every single cell of the paper would coincide with 4 cells from the checkerboard pattern. Antialiasing is when you observe this fact, and fill each 5x5 cell (display pixel) with an _average_ tone of each of the coinciding checkerboard cell (texture pixel). The result will contain various shades of gray rather than just whites and blacks. It is not so crisp, but it is eye-pleasing and realistic.

Produced in September 2007, uploaded in November 2010.

snippet.title: A selection of VGM in Scream Tracker 3.2
snippet.description:
A selection of Video Game Music that I have sequenced as S3M modules entirely by myself or automatically converted from various sources using tools that I have written for the purposes.

Some of these songs are "MIDI-S3M", which are AdLib S3M files wherein the instrument list contains just enough information in ASCII format to enable another S3M player to play them through a MIDI output device. Which is what I did, convert into MIDI and play through TiMiDity++.
For example, the string "GM1:" in an instrument name tells that the S3M player that when playing the module through a MIDI device (or when converting into a MIDI), the instrument is to be considered a piano (General MIDI patch number 1). Other attributes allow finetuning the pitch and volume etc. relative to what the S3M otherwise indicates.
I am not very good at selecting PCM samples -- I mainly concern with the melody and the very general outlines of the instruments' sound  -- which is why I delegate my PCM sample concerns to a synthesizer -- usually AdLib or MIDI. Sometimes the results sound good, othertimes not so good. These may be not my best productions, so I compensated the quality with quantity. :)

As is with most of my videos here on this channel, to better appreciate the show -- as goes for art in general --, you will have to look beyond the immediate content and realize all the work that has made the product possible. For this video, I count at least 7 distinct tool programs that I have written, without which this video would have not been possible. Of course not always is the result worth the effort. But it is good to get to showcase it at least somehow. And that is one of the things what "to live" is about -- to exercise one's talents and passions. Live! Shine!
Do you not know how to shine? Maybe you haven't discovered it yet. Maybe the clues are around you, but someone is yet to put them together. I have had moments like that. When I discover new things that I really enjoy doing and that sort of come naturally, yet never realized it before despite that, in retrospect, signs of it were around for quite some time. Pray for God, our Father who is in Heavens, to show you your talents and to give you the wisdom to put them into use that brings glory to Him. I'm still learning...

snippet.title: Making songs with Scream Tracker 3
snippet.description:
In this video I create two AdLib songs and play a third one that uses PCM samples. My emphasis here is on using various "commands" that control how the tracks are being played, such as the loop opcode (SBn), the note delay opcode (SDn) and the row-delay opcode (SEn). The note cut opcode (SCn) was also going to be used, but unfortunately ST3 does not honor it in AdLib mode.

Apologies about the few scattered mistakes in this video. It is not easy to create music and to verify that it plays as intended when your emulator is running at 30% realtime speed while recording. That is why I script my videos beforehand.  But it is easy to forget things even if you prepare with a script. For the curious, here is the script that I wrote for first song in this video: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/youtubemusic/goo2b.txt

I applied mild reverb and chorus filters over the sound in this video, to approximate the same type of sound that I had when I originally composed these songs on Sound Blaster AWE32. The exact commandline to transform the soundtrack was: sox in.wav out.wav vol 0.7 reverb 30 50 50 chorus 0.5 0.7   40 0.4 0.25 2 -t

The keyboard display and the oscilloscope at the bottom of the screen were added by a patch that I wrote into the emulator, automatically during the recording, directly into the recorded video stream. Unfortunately I have accidentally deleted the source code of that feature, so I cannot make it available for download.

The three (or five) songs in this video are:
-- Twisty passages, all alike (Goonies II). The naming is mine, and the original Konami theme only had two instruments + echo.
-- Optimization 2. It is my original composition.
-- Mountain lands, from NES Solar Jetman. Again the original Tradewest/Rare theme only had two instruments + percussion. My version here is thus heavily altered. Also, it begins with a little shoutout to the Super Mario Bros theme by Koji Kondo. The instruments I used for the mountainland song were ripped from Twn's chip tunes; the instruments in the lead-in were ones I generated with QBasic or by taking pieces from DOS4GW.EXE.
-- The tiny ditty that I play on the sample listing screen with the fast-decaying version of PsiFlute is from Star Tropics, by Y. Hirai.

This video is not education nor is it entertainment, but vaguely maybe a little of both.

snippet.title: Making a song with Scream Tracker 3 and AdLib samples
snippet.description:
This tool-assisted education video demonstrates how to create a simple song using Scream Tracker 3 for MS-DOS with nothing but FM synthesis for the instruments. This time I loaded the AdLib instruments from my library of OPL MIDI patches, and wrote a tracker version of the traditional Jewish song, Va'Yeven Uziahu.

Note: Near the end of the video, I convert the song into a MIDI and play it with TiMiDity++. However, I still don't have means to record+sync Linux audio to DOSBox, so I recorded it separately into a wav file and mixed it in post-process. This is why the oscilloscope does not react during the MIDI playback (and why the song continues even after the Linux simulator (*cough*) is closed). Anything that is reacted by the oscilloscope was really produced during the recording.

Note: It is not really this fast to create songs / arrangements (even if it were not a tool-assisted movie). A lot of it is in experimenting what works and adjusting ad infinitum. I first did all that before I recorded the video; in this video I am merely illustrating the process by manually copying my previous work onto a new clean tracker sheet. This results in a compact video that is nice to watch but still realistic because everything that you see happening really happens.
The reason why I did not catch the obvious transcription error at 3:46 any sooner than I did was because when you're recording a movie and the emulator is running at slow speed, it is rather difficult to hear the details from the choppy sound.

snippet.title: How to create music in C++ from scratch (MIDI file format) / C++11 variadic templates example
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video, I demonstrate how to write a program that creates a MIDI file from scratch. Some basics on how to write music in a computer program are shown. You see me type every line. 

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

MIDI is described in detail in Wikipedia, but put very shortly (and not entirely accurately), its best analogy is in sheet music rather than in an mp3 file. To play MIDI files, you need a synthesizer. There are computer synthesizer programs for various operating systems. In this video, I used an AdLib synthesizer for DOS that I wrote once -- apologies about that -- because I still could not figure out how to record audio from Linux synced to DOSBox's speed, or how to hook TiMidity++ into DOSBox, and DOSBox does not yet even emulate MPU-401 to begin with.
The loopBegin and loopEnd tags are only supported by two MIDI players that I know: FMDRV, which I have created (seen in this video), and Final Fantasy VII by Square Enix. I hold it in a standard's esteem.

Also, as a peculiar quirk, I happen to be running Linux under DOS in this video. I wrote a Linux emulator for DOS using Borland C++ ;-)
Actually, what I wrote is just a (very fast and accurate) terminal emulator; the "simulated" Linux is actually the host computer under which the DOSBox instance runs.
The MHz/GHz rating at the bottom of the screen is the speed by which the CPU emulated by DOSBox runs. I adjust it occasionally during the recording (to make it possible for me to type a long piece of text in a very short time), and the rating is updated in real time.
Also, it is only faintly seen, but I launch a FreeDOS shell at one point. It is why you see two different kind of "DIR" responses in the video.
My editor of choice is neither Vi nor Emacs, but Joseph Allen's Joe. Normally I use 256-color xterm, but here I am running under 16-color DOS and VGA text mode, so the 256-colorness is only emulated by dynamically remapping the palette on demand.
As another peculiar quirk, my Linux "emulator" sets up a 51-line text mode by adding one extra line of text to the screen. Incidentally, I discovered, this mode has a screen resolution of 720x408, which makes it _very_ close to the aspect ratio of 16:9 with square pixels. Hence I set the video aspect ratio to 16:9 rather than VGA's actual ratio, 4:3.

This is the first programming example for which I did not print a script beforehand. I planned and created this entirely in one evening. Therefore there is no PDF to download. But you can download the MIDI file produced by the program, here: https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/midimake.mid (it is my original composition).
The source code that I typed in this video can be downloaded here:
https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/midimake.cc

You can find the DOSBox Linux terminal hack here:
-- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/src/patch-dosbox-forkpty.txt -- This patch must be applied into DOSBox.
-- https://bisqwit.iki.fi/src/linux_for_dosbox_snapshot-2011-12-08.zip -- This is the terminal program that is run in DOSBox. Note that it uses hard-coded Finnish keyboard layout. It requires that DOSBox is patched using the above patch.

snippet.title: Writing a Tetris clone in GW-BASIC -- Tandy 1000 programming example
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video I demonstrate how to create a Tetris clone in GW-BASIC, a programming language tool written by Microsoft. You see me type every line.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/RealBisqwit
Patreon: https://patreon.com/Bisqwit (alternatives at https://iki.fi/bisqwit/donate.html)
Twitch: https://twitch.tv/RealBisqwit
Homepage: https://iki.fi/bisqwit/

Microsoft GW-BASIC and Basica are the predecessors to QBasic, which was a popular programming tool shipped without extra charge with MS-DOS versions 4 through 5.
In those days, it was de-facto standard to provide a computer with a BASIC interpreter. Those days are no longer, but in my opinion, even today, BASIC remains one of the easiest platforms to start programming something visual. 

In this video, I also demonstrate the multi-channel PC speaker of Tandy 1000 to play some music tunes.

The source code (and the script I used for reference when creating this video) can be found at:

To better understand how this program works, you can read this flowgraph. https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/gwbasictetris_graph.pdf

snippet.title: Creating a MOD / S3M player in C++ [VERSION 2]
snippet.description:
In this tool-assisted education video, I demonstrate how to write a S3M player from scratch.
S3M is music module format improved from MOD, inferior to IT or XM, introduced in Scream Tracker version 3.
You see me type every line. The resulting program supports most of S3M features and special effects, though not all. There might be a bug or two there too, but in most songs I've tested the bugs are well hidden :) Most significant limitations: No AdLib support, and 8-bit mono sound only.

It would be easy to change the program to produce 16-bit stereo signal instead, but then the Sound Blaster interfacing code would have been longer. I would have to use DMA; now I was able to just write to the DAC directly. If I wrote this in Linux using ALSA / OSS, it'd be easier, but at the time when I created this video, that was not possible for me.
It would be flower picking kind of trivial to add AdLib support, too, but I could not reasonably fit that into this time limit, and it would also have changed this into rather exclusively a DOS program. I wanted to keep this cross-platform, aside from the Sound Blaster driver in the beginning of the code.

The only sound in this video is produced by the program that I create in this video.

The songs: Axel F by unknown author; Backwards-sdrawkcaB by FireLight; Satellite One by Purple Motion; Star Control II Hyperspace theme by Riku Nuottajärvi; One Must Fall theme by Kenny Chou; Ode to ProTracker by Asle/Lithium/ReDoX (the credits shown in the video are wrong).

Disclaimer: MS-DOS is not my primary programming platform. Far from it; but DOSBox is a convenient platform to record videos from, so that is why this is a DOS program.

Youtube limits the length of published videos to 10 minutes (though sometimes it allows a bit over that), which is why I rushed this video quite a bit in order to let everything that needs to be shown to be shown.  In particular, when the screen seems to be flashing a lot, I'm just fixing bugs.

The source code (and the script I used for reference when creating this video) can be found at:
https://bisqwit.iki.fi/jutut/kuvat/programming_examples/s3mplayer.pdf
